SCALLOP significantly reduces both training variance and training time while consistently improving performance compared to F2D2, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art while achieving up to 10x inference speedup over the fastest baseline.

authors.name: RuiKang OuYang, Hanlin Yu, Xinyue Ai, Yutong He, Nicholas M. Boffi, Pradeep Ravikumar, Jose Miguel Hernandez-Lobato, Max Simchowitz, Benjamin Kurt Miller, Omar Chehab

papers.title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models produce realistic, prompt-aligned images, but samples for the same prompt often cover only a few visually distinct modes. For person-centric prompts, this lack of diversity can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize representative diversity as target-mode coverage: how well a set of samples covers predefined modes, such as colors or perceived-race categories. We then propose MultiMaxPO, a reinforcement learning post-training method that improves this coverage in diffusion T2I models by optimizing a multi-axis max@K objective. Given one score per mode for each sample, multi-axis max@K takes the maximum over samples for each mode and then sums these maxima. A sample therefore receives credit for a mode only when it raises that mode's maximum, so different samples are rewarded for different modes. We verify this credit assignment on a synthetic Gaussian mixture and on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with pixel-based color rewards, and then apply it to perceived-appearance fairness. On held-out prompts and under three automatic evaluators, MultiMaxPO improves the Fairness Score over the base model by 0.22-0.36 on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and by 0.07-0.19 on FLUX.1-dev, outperforms matched RL baselines, and maintains image quality and text alignment. Code is available at https://github.com/KuOnoda/multi-axis-maxk.

authors.name: Ku Onoda, Paavo Parmas, Hiroki Furuta, Soichiro Nishimori, Yuta Oshima, Shohei Taniguchi, Yutaka Matsuo

papers.title: Volatility-Aware Extreme Event Detection in High-Frequency Financial Markets
papers.summary: Predicting extreme price movements in high-frequency financial markets is a challenging task due to non-stationarity, heavy-tailed return distributions, and severe class imbalance. In particular, rare but impactful events are often difficult to detect using conventional modeling approaches, which typically treat extreme movements as isolated observations. This study proposes a volatility-aware approach for extreme event detection using high-frequency Bitcoin limit order book (LOB) data. Motivated by empirical evidence of volatility clustering, the target formulation is extended to incorporate both large future returns and high-volatility regimes. This redefinition increases the proportion of informative samples and aligns the learning objective with the underlying market dynamics. Using a tree-based model (XGBoost) with time-series cross-validation and imbalance-aware evaluation, the proposed method achieves a Precision-Recall AUC of approximately 0.40, significantly outperforming the baseline formulation with a PR-AUC of around 0.06. This represents more than a sixfold improvement in detecting rare events. The results highlight that target design plays a critical role in financial machine learning, often exceeding the impact of model complexity. By incorporating volatility structure into the labeling process, the proposed approach provides a more effective and realistic framework for extreme event detection in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets.

authors.name: Maorufa Zaman, Haris Md Sahed

papers.title: Optimizing the Preconditioner: A Black-box Online-to-Nonconvex Conversion with Static Regret Minimization Oracles
papers.summary: Stochastic nonconvex optimization is central to training deep networks and LLMs in modern machine learning. We give a black-box reduction from stochastic nonconvex optimization to ordinary static regret minimization in online convex optimization (OCO), addressing the open problem posed by Chen and Hazan (2024). Our reduction maintains a predictable gradient tracker, while a black-box online learner $\mathcal A$ selects a preconditioner that transforms this tracker into the update direction. Given a $\beta$-smooth function with initial gap at most $M$ and an unbiased gradient oracle with variance bounded by $\sigma^2$, we bound the expected average squared gradient norm by $O(\sigma\sqrt{M\beta/T}+\sqrt{M\beta}\mathrm{Reg}_T(\mathcal A)/T+\frac{M\beta}{T})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_T(\mathcal A)$ is the static regret of $\mathcal A$ against the identity preconditioner. Thus, any OCO oracle with $O(\sqrt T)$ regret recovers the classical $O(T^{-1/2})$ convergence rate. We also prove that the additive variance term cannot be removed: every conversion making a constant number of stochastic-oracle queries per round, whose guarantee is stated through static regret against a comparator that the online learner can play, must contain an additive term of order $\sigma\sqrt{M\beta/T}$ for sufficiently large $T$. Moreover, for every online learner, our conversion bound is tight up to universal constants. We also extend the framework to nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, still relying only on ordinary static regret, and attain the optimal convergence rate for Goldstein-type stationarity. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments on nonconvex objectives to illustrate how the reduction exploits online-selected preconditioners while using the same stochastic-oracle budget as stochastic gradient descent.

authors.name: Haichen Hu, David Simchi-Levi

papers.title: Beyond Single-Episode Optimization: Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding for Long-Term Advertising Effectiveness
papers.summary: Auto-bidding systems optimize bids to maximize value under efficiency constraints such as Cost-Per-Action (CPA). Existing methods treat each day as an independent episode. However, many advertisers produce value so sparsely that per-day efficiency ratios become statistically unreliable, undermining advertiser retention. Platforms therefore evaluate window-level efficiency over sliding windows of $W{=}7$ days, ensuring fair evaluation and long-term advertising effectiveness. This creates cross-episode coupling: each day's bidding decisions affect up to $W$ overlapping windows, so setting daily targets requires anticipating future market conditions. We propose SWAG-Bid (Sliding-Window Aware Generative Auto-Bidding), a hierarchical framework decomposing this challenge into episode-level planning and step-level execution. The planner uses a Masked Trajectory Model to forecast markets and generate candidate plans, scored across all overlapping windows by Multi-Window Model Predictive Control Sampling (MWMS) with exponential confidence decay. The controller adjusts reliance on this guidance through a state-adaptive gate, Per-Step Gated Adaptive Layer Normalization (PSG-AdaLN), complemented by Return-to-Go and Cost-to-Go channels carrying budget and constraint information. Experiments on AuctionNet-Sparse and online A/B tests on AliExpress show that SWAG-Bid achieves competitive constraint satisfaction and value acquisition under sliding-window evaluation.

authors.name: Binglin Wu, Chuan Yue, Yingyi Zhang, Xianneng Li, Ruyue Deng, Weiru Zhang, Xiaoyi Zeng

papers.title: Power law graph attention: exact generalization of scaled dot-product attention, empirical collapse at inference
papers.summary: The Large Language Model from Power Law Decoder Representations (PLDR-LLM) and its attention, Power Law Graph Attention (PLGA), replace the fixed bilinear form of scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) with a learned, input-generated bilinear operator $G_{\mathrm{LM}}$, built from a positive tensor $A_{\mathrm{LM}}$ by elementwise power laws. The architecture is fully specified, verified against pinned reference releases; claims are labeled theorem, conditional theorem, measurement, or conjecture. Unconditionally: PLGA contains SDPA exactly at $G_{\mathrm{LM}}=I$; $A_{\mathrm{LM}}$ and $A_{P}$ are strictly entrywise positive, with Perron-Frobenius structure on $A_{\mathrm{LM}}$; the DAG regularizer has the NOTEARS walk-counting form and positivity obstructs exact acyclicity; and, under nonresonance (satisfied by standard rotary frequencies), a commutant criterion identifies which operators preserve relative-position dependence. An inference-collapse theorem: exact input invariance of the head score operators $G_{\mathrm{LM}}$ collapses inference to generalized SDPA with a constant operator per head. Measured invariance: relative fluctuations of $10^{-6}$ and below; perturbation bounds quantify but do not certify cached inference; the assembled proxy misses the decoding margin. A conditional three-stage mechanism (rotary twirl, concentration, row-map contraction) is measured on a released checkpoint. Blockwise training and scoring under the global Gram are stated with explicit target exposure; on tested samples, block and sequential scoring select identical answers and agree on the published TruthfulQA probability-mass metric within $5\times10^{-5}$ per item. Self-organized criticality enters as a phenomenological framework with an intrinsic order parameter; open claims become falsifiable conjectures. Selected proof cores are machine-checked in Lean 4.

authors.name: Burc Gokden

papers.title: An Efficient Minimax-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial $m$-Set Bandits
papers.summary: We study adversarial combinatorial bandits with $m$-set actions, where at each round the learner selects $m$ out of $d$ items and observes only the aggregate loss of the selected items. The resulting action set contains $K=\binom{d}{m}$ elements and can therefore be exponentially large. We propose a computationally efficient algorithm that exploits this structure without explicitly enumerating the action set. Against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries, it guarantees, with probability at least $1-\delta$, regret against the best action in hindsight of $R_T =O(\sqrt{dT\log(K/\delta)}). $ This matches the high-probability regret bound of the finite-action EXP3 with Kiefer-Wolfowitz exploration algorithm of Zimmert and Lattimore, whose direct implementation may require exponential space. Our algorithm instead represents each sampling distribution with $d$ parameters and runs in polynomial time without enumerating the action set. This resolves an open problem posed by Maiti et al. We complement this upper bound with a matching high-probability lower bound. For all sufficiently small $\delta$ and all sufficiently large horizons, every randomized algorithm admits an adaptive non-anticipating adversary for which, with probability at least $\delta$, $R_T=\Omega( \sqrt{dT\log(K/\delta)}). $ Thus, the rate is minimax optimal up to universal constants in this regime. In particular, setting $m=1$ shows that the $\log K$ factor in the high-probability regret bound for ordinary $K$-armed bandits against adaptive non-anticipating adversaries is unavoidable. This strengthens the lower bound of Gerchinovitz and Lattimore, closing the remaining $\sqrt{\log K}$ gap between high-probability upper and lower regret bounds.

authors.name: Francesco Bacchiocchi, Tommaso Cesari, Roberto Colomboni

papers.title: Sparse Koopman Autoencoders Identify Local Dynamical Regimes in Multibasin Systems
papers.summary: Koopman autoencoders (KAEs) seek a higher-dimensional latent representation in which nonlinear dynamics evolve linearly. However, many interesting systems have multiple basins of attraction, and both theoretical and empirical work has shown these multibasin systems cannot generally admit a single finite-dimensional global Koopman embedding under standard assumptions. We posit that encoders with a sparsity-inducing objective encouraging few active latent coefficients will provide latent supports as an inspectable basin-modeling principle for Koopman autoencoders. We use these encoders producing sparse latents in training Sparse Koopman Autoencoders (SKAEs) without basin labels or other regime annotations, and treat the learned latent supports as model-produced regime variables after training. Across a range of procedurally generated multibasin systems and chaotic flows, we show that SKAEs have superior forecasting performance compared to dense-latent KAEs. We also perform a mechanistic study that shows latent supports produced by SKAEs are both essential for the quality of the representation and useful for identifying basins on basin-interior states, whereas dense-latent KAEs collapse to an uninformative single support family. These results identify sparse latents and their corresponding supports as label-free, interpretable regime variables for Koopman learning in nonlinear systems with multiple local dynamical laws.

authors.name: Aidan Li, Uday Kiran Reddy Tadipatri, Mahan Fathi, Sarath Chandar, Ross Goroshin

papers.title: DeSyR: A decoupled symbolic recovery framework for PDEs with PINN-guided structure discovery and physics-based coefficient refinement
papers.summary: Recovering explicit symbolic solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) from physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) is attractive, yet selecting and fitting expressions against neural predictions can lock the recovered solution into the teacher's approximation error. We propose DeSyR (Decoupled Symbolic Recovery) to break this dependence. DeSyR uses PINNs only to discover candidate structures and initial coefficient estimates; once a structure is fixed, the governing equations and constraints alone determine the refined coefficients. Multiple candidates with different fitting-error--complexity trade-offs are retained, evaluated after physics-only refinement, and reduced to the simplest expression within a physically near-optimal set. Joint refinement extends the same principle to coupled fields. For fixed candidate parameterizations, affine error identities and local nonlinear analysis show how teacher errors enter fitted coefficients and establish conditions under which physical residuals control coefficient and solution errors. Across seven benchmarks covering scalar evolution equations, multidimensional elliptic problems and coupled incompressible flows, DeSyR attains mean relative solution errors on the order of $10^{-14}$ or smaller and lower reported mean physical residuals than PINNs, physics-informed symbolic networks and teacher-fitted symbolic distillation. With the expression structure held fixed, estimating coefficients from physical constraints further yields more accurate frequency estimates and solutions than fitting teacher predictions. DeSyR therefore turns neural approximations into guides for structure discovery, while physical constraints determine the final explicit solution.

authors.name: Pancheng Niu, Jun Guo, Qiaolin He, Jingcai Guo, Yanchao Shi

papers.title: Import What You Need: Learning When and How to Augment EHR Graphs with External Knowledge
papers.summary: Longitudinal prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) is limited by the sparsity and irregularity in patient trajectories, and knowledge augmentation with external knowledge graphs (KGs) offers a promising way to alleviate these issues. However, KG expansion often follows predefined rules, with limited control over whether and how to augment each visit as a patient's state evolves. We propose ReTA, a Reinforcement learning-based dynamic Topology Augmentation framework that casts KG import as a per-visit, budget-aware policy. ReTA first constructs an offline refined pool of KG-grounded templates, then learns a policy to select one augment action per visit from three options: Soft Import, which enriches node features without modifying graph topology, Hard Import, which grafts a compact KG subgraph onto the visit graph to create message-passing shortcuts, and Skip, which leaves the visit unaugmented when the base encoder is already confident. To stabilize learning, ReTA employs a decoupled encoder that processes semantic and structural signals in separate channels and fuses them via adaptive gating. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV across diagnosis prediction, mortality, and readmission show that ReTA consistently outperforms strong baselines while remaining efficient, with larger gains under sparse supervision. ReTA transfers across datasets and knowledge graphs and yields interpretable augmentation patterns.

authors.name: Chen Chen, Mohsen Nayebi Kerdabadi, Dongjie Wang, Mei Liu, Zijun Yao

papers.title: Budgeted Task-Aware Acquisition of Dynamic Networks
papers.summary: Learning on dynamic graphs is difficult when changes in the underlying network are only partially observed. Acquiring current graph information incurs observation and computational costs, making complete updates impractical under limited resources. This paper focuses on budgeted task-aware acquisition on dynamic networks, where a model needs to decide which stale graph information to refresh for a downstream task. We propose Scout, a lightweight framework that learns the task value of querying each node from the maintained graph and observation history. Our evaluation covers one synthetic and 4 real-world dynamic networks, 2 downstream tasks, 9 acquisition baselines, and several query budgets. Scout achieves the highest mean downstream performance in 15 of the 21 benchmark-budget settings and ranks within the top two in 19 of them. Its average rank is 1.4, compared with 3.2 for the strongest baseline. On the same dynamic network, task-matched acquisition improves link-prediction AUC by 0.005-0.007 and node-classification accuracy by 0.007-0.017 over task-mismatched acquisition. These results show that useful graph observations depend on the downstream task and that limited observation budgets can be allocated effectively by learning directly from downstream utility.

authors.name: Zihe Zhou

papers.title: Online Draft Co-Training for Speculative Decoding in Large-Scale, Long-Context RL Post-Training
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates rollout generation, which dominates the cost of reinforcement learning (RL) post-training. Online co-training keeps the draft aligned with the evolving policy, further increasing acceptance length and speedup. However, training large models on long contexts requires context parallelism (CP) and pipeline parallelism (PP), and co-training drafts under this layout poses two obstacles: (1) the draft's branch attention is unsupported by causal CP, and (2) the target features that the draft consumes are spread across PP stages. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of online draft co-training in NeMo-RL. For CP, we extend packed, load-balanced zigzag ring attention by merging rank-local branch attention with causal main-sequence attention. For PP, TapChannel transports intermediate target features across stages via a separate path, leaving the pipeline schedule unaffected. Experiments show that co-training keeps the policy's reward and accuracy close to the no-draft baseline while delivering $1.48$--$2.25\times$ rollout speedups and $1.19$--$1.88\times$ end-to-end training speedups across model scales up to 122B. Our CP design achieves strong scaling at 256K sequence length with significant memory savings over prior work, and our PP transport incurs modest overhead. Code can be found at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/issues/3698.

authors.name: Zili Wang, Zhaopeng Qiu, Yuekai Zhang, Shuang Yu, Seonjin Na, Hayate Iso, Junjie Lai

papers.title: Literati: Towards Anytime Optimal Shape Generalized Trees via AO*
papers.summary: Decision trees are prized for their interpretability and strong performance on tabular data, but popular greedy top-down induction algorithms can yield suboptimal and unnecessarily complex structures. Optimal decision tree methods address this through global optimization, yet remain restricted to axis-aligned threshold splits, which limit the expressivity of each node and often force deep, complex trees to capture non-linear feature effects. Shape Generalized Trees (SGTs) generalize threshold splits to learnable univariate shape functions, improving expressivity and enabling more compact trees. However, existing SGT induction algorithms are greedy and offer no optimality guarantees. In this work, we introduce Literati, the first algorithm for optimal SGT induction. We propose a novel AND/OR graph formulation of the problem that jointly optimizes tree structure and shape function complexity. To solve this AND/OR graph, we develop an AO*-based algorithm with two enhancements that improve anytime performance while preserving optimality: a secondary heuristic for OR-node selection and a round-robin policy for AND-node exploration. Across 24 real-world datasets, Literati achieves higher training and test accuracy than state-of-the-art tree approaches.

authors.name: Nakul Upadhya, Eldan Cohen

papers.title: TabPFN-3.5: Technical Report
papers.summary: We introduce TabPFN-3.5, our new flagship Tabular Foundation Model. It significantly outperforms its predecessor, TabPFN-3, and all existing baselines across a broad range of tabular problems. TabPFN-3.5 sets a new state of the art on standard tabular prediction in TabArena, and extends it to the data practitioners encounter in practice: non-i.i.d. data with temporal or grouped splits, tables with strings, text and images, high-cardinality categorical features, and wide tables with many features. These gains carry over to our task-specific harnesses: state of the art on relational data and stronger time-series forecasting. For faster inference, our variant TabPFN-3.5-Fast runs up to 3x faster than TabPFN-3 while keeping most of the accuracy gains. In addition, we upgrade TabPFN-3.5-Plus, expanding our multimodal capabilities with advanced text and date handling alongside proprietary inference optimizations. Finally, we release a new version of our Thinking mode, TabPFN-3.5-Thinking, which scales inference-time computation to push the state of the art further. It benefits from our stronger base model and from inference-time improvements that make it up to 12x faster than TabPFN-3-Thinking.

authors.name: Benjamin J\"ager, Nick Erickson, L\'eo Grinsztajn, Felix Birkel, Klemens Fl\"oge, Oscar Key, K\"ur\c{s}at Kaya, Jonas K\"ubler, Ad\`ele Frankel, Tobias Schr\"oder, Anurag Garg, Jan Hendrik Metzen, David Salinas, Simon Bing, Kristina Collins, Tuana \c{C}elik, Vahid Balazadeh, Lydia Sidhoum, Tom\'as Pereda, Brendan Roof, Andrej Tschalzev, Siyuan Guo, Philipp Singer, Lennart Purucker, Jake Robertson, Marie Salmon, Philipp Jund, Jerry Chen, Diana Kriuchkova, Arthur Cahu, Eliott Kalfon, Adrian Hayler, Georg Grab, Vitor Monteiro, Lilly Wehrhahn, Dominik Safaric, Clara Cornu, Alan Arazi, Rylee Grace, Simone Alessi, Mihir Manium, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Yann LeCun, Madelon Hulsebos, Sauraj Gambhir, Noah Hollmann, Frank Hutter

papers.title: Uncertainty and Business-Aware Remaining Useful Life Estimation for Semiconductor Manufacturing
papers.summary: Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimates guide maintenance in semiconductor manufacturing, where a late intervention can disrupt production but an early one discards usable equipment life. A single prediction does not express the uncertainty needed to choose between these outcomes. We combine Deep Learning (DL) sequence models with Simoultaneous Quantile Regression (SQR) to estimate RUL at selectable quantile levels, and evaluate maintenance decisions using Unexpected Breaks (UB), Unexploited Lifetime (UL), and a cost-weighted objective. On the $F_1$ fault mode of the 2018 PHM Data Challenge (PHM18) ion-milling dataset, we compare recurrent, Transformer, and State Space Models (SSM) architectures. Diagonal State Spaced (S4D) gives the strongest overall RUL accuracy across the evaluated quantiles. Varying the quantile and maintenance window exposes the trade-off between failure risk and early intervention; under the examined cost ratios, the resulting decisions have lower cost than the Preventive Maintenance (PvM) baselines.

authors.name: Davide Frizzo, Francesco Borsatti, Gian Antonio Susto

papers.title: A Concentration Bound for Two-Timescale Actor-Critic Algorithm
papers.summary: Significant research effort has been directed in recent years towards establishing both asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for two-timescale actor--critic algorithms, where the actor recursion is run on a slower timescale than the critic recursion. This work derives a uniform all-time concentration bound for the actor--critic algorithm with function approximation in the long-run average-reward setting. This bound helps us analyze the behavior of the actor parameter with high probability. We show that, after some finite time, the actor parameter enters a safe region and remains within it thereafter with high probability. Specifically, with probability at least $1-\epsilon_1-\epsilon_2$, the actor error $\Vert \theta_k-\theta^{*}\Vert$ is $O\left(\frac{n_0^{3/4}}{k}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon_2}}+\left(\frac{1}{n_0}\right)^{1/4}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon_1}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{n_0}\right)^{1/4}\right)$ for all $k\geq n_0$ and sufficiently large $n_0$. We also present experimental results demonstrating that the aforementioned actor error diminishes with the number of actor-parameter updates.

authors.name: Prashansa Panda, Shalabh Bhatnagar

papers.title: Bayesian Optimization with Fisher Information Geometry: Gradient Bounds and Trust-Region Methods
papers.summary: We study Bayesian optimization (BO) through the lens of information geometry. Pulling back the Fisher information metric through the surrogate posterior map yields a local sensitivity tensor on the input space, which leads to an upper bound on the gradient of reparameterizable acquisition functions (AFs). This view explains vanishing-gradient behavior in high-dimensional BO and provides a common interpretation of heuristics such as RAASP and dimension-scaled lengthscales. The upper bound can also serve as a generic recipe to understand the behavior of new acquisition functions or surrogates in high input dimensions as well. Using the bounds, we also identify necessary conditions for an input location to be an optimizer of the AF for a univariate Gaussian predictive posterior. Building on this analysis, we propose FITR, a trust-region-based BO method that replaces lengthscale-based scaling with local pullback-Fisher weights. FITR is not restricted to GP kernels with explicit lengthscales and easily generalizes to non-isotropic surrogates. FITR shows competitive performance on several benchmarks.

authors.name: Saksham Kiroriwal, Julius Pfrommer, J\"urgen Beyerer

papers.title: From Perturbation Sensitivity to Sparse Autoencoder Feature Interpretation: An EEG Foundation-Model Case Study
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) split a model's internal activity into many sparse units, or latents, and a latent is often named after a concept when removing that concept from the input changes its activity. We identify a consequential confound in this inference: if removing the concept changes the input more than the comparison edit does, a larger response may reflect a larger edit rather than the concept. Brain-signal (electroencephalography, EEG) models provide a controlled test, because how much an edit changes the EEG input can be measured directly. We measure the SAE response as the change in how often each latent is active, averaged over all latents. Across 27 combinations of model, dataset, and layer, removing the 8--12 Hz alpha band changes this response 7.33 times as much as removing an equally wide 30--34 Hz control band, but it also changes the signal far more. Matching the two edits per trial on squared time-domain distortion lowers the mean ratio to 1.42, with 19 of 27 combinations above one. Matching thus substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, the alpha--control contrast. The residual supports relative sensitivity under this single control, not general spectral specificity or an individual alpha-representing latent. We use an evidence-to-claim map to separate what this comparison supports from stronger claims of specificity and feature semantics.

authors.name: Yucong Cao, Chenqi Li, Tingting Zhu

papers.title: Training and Inference Dynamics of PLDR-LLMs: Row-Map Collapse, Renormalization, and Predictive Reduction
papers.summary: This monograph develops a unified account of training and inference in Power Law Decoder Representation language models (PLDR-LLMs). Exact finite work identities decompose changes in the absolute energy of the row-centered learned map into parameter contributions, signed interactions, and numerical observation defects. Positive affine blocking retains restarts at the row-constant face, while the augmented AdamW state supplies the complete dynamical description. Predictive renormalization acts on the complete conditional training law for a single pass over distinct corpus target blocks, retaining optimizer memory, remaining data, schedule, and numerical policy. Autonomous reductions require closure; approximate reductions carry successor and emission errors. Finite-population covariance, matched physical clocks, matrix fluxes, and signed temporal energy connect row dynamics to model-wide observations. Absolute row collapse, relative row concentration, operator stabilization, and predictive accuracy are distinguished. Experiments reveal observer and optimizer dependence, reject the tested autonomous row-state candidates, and support finite conditional prediction and state-specific operator reduction. Independent single-pass families exhibit moving finite fluctuation regions without establishing a thermodynamic critical class. Conditional symmetry, head limits, covariance flows, and readout error budgets specify assumptions needed to transfer scaling laws to inference. The theory separates exact identities, conditional dynamical claims, and finite empirical findings, with proofs, selected formal checks, and compact numerical evidence.

authors.name: Burc Gokden

papers.title: ORBIT-FMIB: Tracking Order-Resolved Epistatic Information Through ESM-2
papers.summary: Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance alone does not reveal which forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. We ask whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy, introducing ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method is validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before being applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations. An initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information ($\Delta_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.107$). An independent replication of the complete measurement grid, under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, substantially reduced this contrast ($\Delta_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.017$), and its sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics ($-0.011$ to $+0.015$). We therefore do not currently have robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its documented removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and is unaffected by this finding. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models; this study's own replication result illustrates why such probing requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before its output is treated as a biological finding.

authors.name: Maryam Rahimimovassagh, Waldemar Karwowski, Ivan Garibay, Niloofar Yousefi

papers.title: The Implicit Bias of Hyperbolic Representation Learning for Multiclass Data: A Busemann Risk Perspective
papers.summary: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $\mu$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\tfrac12\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that large-radius directions can approach critical points of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb H^n$, even during radial return. These results provide a rigorous large-radius perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.

authors.name: Xingrun Li, Sho Kuno, Yusuke Mukuta, Xin Yang, Tatsuya Harada

papers.title: CausalBind: Causal Modeling and Learning for Protein-Molecule Virtual Screening
papers.summary: Protein-molecule virtual screening is increasingly cast as a problem of representation learning in a shared embedding space. Existing methods rely on dense holistic alignment, entangling invariant binding determinants with nuisance correlations and limiting transfer to new targets. Binding in protein-molecule systems involves sparse cross-modality interactions: binding is governed by a small contact interface and a few decisive local interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and salt bridges) rather than the global structures of the protein and molecule. We hypothesize that uncovering and leveraging sparse interaction patterns is critical for generalization beyond the training data, as these patterns are reusable and expected to improve performance across different scenarios. Since the training data contain only observed binding pairs, we formalize this prior via a V-structure causal model under Heckman-style selection, and establish three theoretical results: (i) when the compatibility between concepts is bilinear, the latent concepts of interacting proteins and molecules are not identifiable, even if the interaction is sparse; (ii) with a non-bilinear compatibility function, these concepts and their sparse interaction support are component-wise identifiable under a sparse antichain condition; and (iii) a low-rank relaxation yields subspace identifiability of the interaction modes, and applies to bilinear compatibility as well. Inspired by these principles, we propose CausalBind with three implementation variants. Extensive experiments on DUD-E and LIT-PCBA benchmarks show that all variants consistently outperform strong retrieval baselines, with the largest gains on LIT-PCBA early enrichment, and further generalize to target- and scaffold-level out-of-distribution splits. Code and scripts are freely available at https://github.com/lokali/CausalBind.

authors.name: Loka Li, Jin Tian, Kun Zhang

papers.title: Shared Geometry As A Rosetta Stone: Cross-Modal Alignment Without Paired Data
papers.summary: Multimodal representations enable zero-shot classification and retrieval, but aligning independently trained models usually requires large amounts of paired data. Yet, the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that models trained on different modalities may converge spontaneously toward a shared representation geometry. But then, do we even need paired examples for cross-modal alignment? Remarkably, we show that paired examples are unnecessary for coarse cross-modal alignment. Our simple Wasserstein Procrustes method with a coarse geometric initialization (GeoWarP) aligns two disjoint embedding sets by estimating a single orthogonal map without seeing any pairs. Across datasets, modalities, and unimodal models, we show that we can consistently align independently trained representations without pairs, and standard geometric alignment metrics accurately predict when this is possible. Nevertheless, we can naturally benefit from paired examples. In the very few-pair regime, our method substantially outperforms existing ones, while staying competitive with pair-based methods with more added examples. Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting alignments can enable text-to-image generation without paired examples. These results show that independently trained models often share enough geometry to establish cross-modal correspondence with little or no paired data.

authors.name: Dominik Schnaus, Thomas Dag\`es, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang, Phillip Isola

papers.title: SPERA: Spherical Prior EEG Foundation Model with Geometry- and Frequency-Aware Latent Prediction
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive measure of ongoing neural activity, but building general-purpose EEG models remains challenging due to the heterogeneity of subjects, devices, and electrode montages. Existing EEG foundation models predominantly rely on reconstruction-based objectives defined on the observed signal, which contains both neural and non-neural components. We introduce the Spherical Prior EEG Representation Architecture (SPERA), an EEG foundation model that adopts the joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to predict in latent space. SPERA introduces a Legendre-polynomial spatial prior, incorporated into attention to encode varying scalp electrode geometries. Two further components adapt the model to EEG: factorized temporal and spatial attention interleaved with periodic full-attention blocks, and a relational spectral regularizer aligning latent similarity structure with spectral views. Pretrained on approximately 80,000 hours of EEG from 29,048 subjects across 106 datasets, SPERA achieves the highest average balanced accuracy across nine downstream tasks spanning clinical, cognitive, and BCI applications. SPERA further exhibits strong parameter efficiency under linear probing and robustness across varying recording conditions, suggesting its potential as a general-purpose backbone for diverse EEG analyses.

authors.name: Minsu Kim, Ye-Sung Kim, Hyeseong Jeon, Wooseok Hyung, Joshua Lee, Chang-Hwan Im

papers.title: Imitation Dominates Reinforcement: Direct In-Context RL Is Closer to ICL Than RL
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly improve at inference time by accumulating experience in context rather than by updating parameters. This process is often described as in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). Whether in-context learning (ICL) can actually play the role of RL, however, has not been tested. We study this question in its simplest form, direct ICRL, where the model conditions directly on raw trajectory-reward pairs, and ask whether the reward acts as a learning signal. Through controlled experiments on four benchmarks across six models, we find that the reward is read, but its effect is small: flipping, randomizing, or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged, and this holds even under meta-prompts that explicitly instruct the model to explore, exploit, or reason over rewards. Trajectories drive improvement, but not through their semantic content: shuffled or corrupted trajectories work as well as real ones. These patterns closely mirror those known in ICL, suggesting that direct ICRL is better understood as a special case of ICL than as inference-time RL. This reframing has implications for agent memory design: ICL factors such as input distribution and demonstrations may matter more than RL elements such as reward shaping and exploration.

authors.name: Minchan Kwon, Seunghee Koh, Sunghyun Baek, Minsung Bae, Junmo Kim

papers.title: Example-driven Parametrisations for Bayesian Shape Optimisation
papers.summary: Bayesian optimisation is the natural tool for shape design when objectives are expensive and non-differentiable, but it needs a compact yet expressive parameterisation of the search space. Hand-crafting one is a complex endeavour requiring domain expertise, and often yields implicit infeasible regions, artificial bounds, and coupled, unordered coordinates. We instead learn the parameterisation from a collection of existing designs, applying principal component analysis to the deformations between shapes. The result is a linear, interpretable search space in which the number of components explicitly trades expressivity against dimensionality. Across aerofoils, wings, and radio-frequency cavities, spanning 2D geometry to 3D aerodynamics and electromagnetics, we show improved sample efficiency and the ability to explore beyond the confines of hand-crafted baselines.

authors.name: Gabriel Diaz-Aylwin, Joseph Neighbour, Abiel Malkani Talwar, Rui-Yang Zhang, Henry B. Moss

papers.title: S$^3$R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution. Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.

authors.name: Yuhang He, Hongyu Ge, Zihan Lin, Siyi Liu, Yongqi Zhang

papers.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
papers.summary: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

authors.name: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov

papers.title: TStruct: Learning Shared Temporal Structures for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Long-term time series forecasting requires learning temporal dependencies that remain stable and generalizable under temporal distribution shifts. However, real-world time series are often noisy, non-stationary, and heterogeneous, making deep learning models prone to overfitting incidental temporal interactions in the training data. This raises a question: when observations are difficult to align, could temporal relationships be easier to reuse? To investigate this possibility, we analyze patch-level temporal relationship matrices across commonly used time series datasets, revealing dominant patterns shared across different temporal windows and variables. Comparisons with patch-shuffled and IID Gaussian controls further support the presence of reusable temporal relationship structures. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textbf{T}emporal \textbf{Struct}ure Network (\textbf{TStruct}), a simple yet effective network that learns reusable temporal dependency structures and adaptively combines them for each sample and variable. Specifically, TStruct directly parameterizes a set of shared temporal dependency matrices and generates normalized combination weights using dynamic sample information and static variable priors. These weights represent a soft allocation of each sample-variable pair over shared temporal dependency structures, enabling the model to generate adaptive temporal dependency matrices under shared structural constraints, rather than fitting incidental interactions in a fully unconstrained manner. Notably, TStruct consistently outperforms several strong baselines across all evaluated datasets, achieving superior accuracy while maintaining high computational efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/yangzeli/TStruct.

authors.name: Yangze Li, Zhengyang Zhou, Qihe Huang, Pengkun Wang, Binwu Wang, Yang Wang

papers.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
papers.summary: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, without explicitly requiring their representations to preserve how the underlying signals evolve. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in Lotus, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, Lotus achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that Lotus uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25-50 times their size on TSRBench. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DA2I2-SLM/Lotus

authors.name: Van Dai Do, Huu Hiep Nguyen, Minh Hoang Nguyen, Manh Nguyen, Hung Le

papers.title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
papers.summary: Must the dimension and accuracy costs of zeroth-order optimization multiply? Global upper bounds for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization scale as $O(d\epsilon^{-4})$, with both factors separately necessary. We show that their product is unavoidable. We establish an $\Omega(d\epsilon^{-4})$ lower bound for smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, yielding an $\Omega(d\delta^{-1}\epsilon^{-3})$ bound for nonsmooth Goldstein stationarity. Both match the best-known full-space upper bounds, establishing joint minimax optimality in dimension and accuracy. These bounds hold against fully adaptive randomized algorithms with unrestricted queries and outputs, even under arbitrary sample reuse. As a byproduct, we establish noiseless exact-value lower bounds for both smooth and Goldstein stationarity, even against randomized algorithms.

authors.name: Yuxuan Xia, Xiao-Tong Yuan

papers.title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
papers.summary: Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

authors.name: Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, Shayan Pardis, Jure Leskovec

papers.title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
papers.summary: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to predicting complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias limits their ability to reconstruct fine-scale flow variations around geometric features such as side mirrors and wheel arches. Reliable assessment of local geometric changes therefore requires models that capture fine spatial detail together with global flow interactions. Inspired by iterative refinement and state evolution, we propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that integrates local multiscale information into global flow modeling. The method extracts local feature variations and encodes them as zeroth- to second-order geometric moments. These encodings are combined with information from earlier layers to form a cross-layer memory. Memory-derived corrections enter the value branch of Physics-Attention, allowing local details to inform global physical-state interactions throughout the network. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. Relative error reductions average 8.72% compared with the best baseline for each metric. Also achieves the lowest high-frequency spectral errors across all five metrics, with an average relative reduction of 16.06% compared with the best baseline. These results support cross-layer reuse of local information for fine-scale automotive flow prediction.

authors.name: Jianglong Liu, Zhicheng Zhu, Jia Hao, Liangyue Jia, Wenxuan He

papers.title: Scaling Graph Reasoning in Language Models with Learnable Graph Positional Encodings
papers.summary: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings.

authors.name: Javier Porras-Valenzuela, Arush Arora, Alejandro Ribeiro

papers.title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace
papers.summary: Low curvature trace, an effective rank condition, is a common explanation for why randomized zeroth-order methods scale to high-dimensional tasks such as language model fine-tuning. Can deterministic methods achieve the same savings? We show that they cannot. We study finding $\varepsilon$-stationary points of $L$-smooth nonconvex functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ from exact function values, assuming that below the starting value the Hessian is dominated by a fixed matrix with trace at most $LE$; this is a fixed-matrix form of the effective rank condition used to explain zeroth-order fine-tuning. When $ET\le d$, the Gaussian two-point method that such fine-tuning uses needs only $O(ET)$ calls if it rejects steps that raise $f$, where $T=L\Delta/\varepsilon^2$ is the iteration count of gradient descent from initial gap $\Delta$, and we prove that every randomized method needs $\Omega(ET)$ calls, so this cost is optimal up to constants. In contrast, every deterministic method needs $\widetilde\Omega(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$ calls, and adaptive subspace search attains $O(d\min\{T,\sqrt{ET}\})$: a deterministic method pays about $d$ calls per discovered direction, and the trace budget allows about $\sqrt{ET}$ directions. Determinism thus multiplies the cost by a factor of order $d/(E+\sqrt{ET})$ up to logarithmic factors, which grows linearly with $d$ for fixed $E$ and $T$; once $E$ exceeds $T$ by a logarithmic factor, deterministic methods need $\Omega(dT)$ calls, as without any trace budget. Our lower bounds hold for $C^\infty$ functions with the matrix bound on all of $\mathbb{R}^d$, even when each call also returns gradient projections priced by rank.

authors.name: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia

papers.title: TPO: Tri-level Distributionally Robust Learning for OOD Direct Preference Optimization
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) minimizes empirical risk over observed preference comparisons, implicitly assuming that the training preference distribution matches the deployment preference distribution. In practice, this distributional assumption often fails, as preference distribution shifts can arise at three levels: group-level shift, prompt-level shift, and preference-level shift. Such multi-level distributional mismatch poses a critical challenge for safe LLM deployment, yet existing robust DPO methods typically either model uncertainty over the joint preference distribution or focus on individual sources of shift, leaving the hierarchical structure of OOD preference shifts underexplored. We propose TPO, a tri-level distributionally robust framework for OOD preference alignment, which jointly models all three levels of distributional uncertainty through a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set. By instantiating it with Wasserstein distance, we derive a tractable and interpretable objective that combines a preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each governed by an independent radius. We establish finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirically validate the effectiveness of TPO across diverse OOD environments.

authors.name: Chengtao Jian, Kai Yang

papers.title: Online Open-World Wafer Defect Discovery using Hyperdimensional Computing
papers.summary: Conventional wafer defect analysis relies on offline, closed-world classifiers that fail to detect novel, unseen defect signatures emerging during continuous semiconductor manufacturing. To address this, we propose WaferHDC, an online open-world wafer defect discovery framework based on hyperdimensional computing (HDC). The memory-centric architecture of WaferHDC enables rapid anomaly detection and grouping of recurring failures into compact hypervector representations. This allows the memory space to dynamically scale with new defect modes without retraining a static classifier or archiving entire raw wafer history. WaferHDC first models normal spatial distributions, then dynamically groups recurring failures into persistent defect memory without labels or predefined class counts. It outperforms the strongest online baseline by 13.3 p.p. in adjusted Rand index and 10.5 p.p. in normalized mutual information on the industry-standard WM-811K dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of WaferHDC for continuous and open-world wafer defect analysis.

authors.name: Quanling Zhao, Ava Emami, Tsuyoshi Id\'e, Rajiv Joshi, Steven Holmes, Michael Passow, Tajana Rosing

papers.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
papers.summary: Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$. For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.

authors.name: Shihao Shao, Dacheng Tao

papers.title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
papers.summary: We study the last iterate of clipped SGD, and of every rule that queries its current iterate and steps along the resulting stochastic gradient, when training is stopped at a data-dependent time, so that guarantees must hold at all times simultaneously. On smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed noise with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1\beta_p$, even with adaptive step sizes and thresholds. This rate lies between the optimal rate $O(T^{-\alpha_p})$ for a known horizon $T$, $\alpha_p=(p-1)/p$, and the previous time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ (Chezhegov et al., ICLR 2026); under finite variance, the exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Their conjecture that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate thus holds with a known horizon (Liu; Jiang et al.) but fails without one. Querying gradients at the running average attains $\tilde O(t^{-\alpha_p})$ at all times, whereas heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded steps cannot improve on $\beta_p$.

authors.name: Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia

papers.title: TriTile: Three-Tier Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.summary: Attention over tens of thousands of visual tokens dominates the inference of video diffusion transformers (DiTs). Existing methods reduce this cost through sparsity, low precision, or both, but use a single precision for all kept tiles. We observe that the output error introduced by approximation varies widely across tiles. Many tiles can be skipped with little error, others must be computed but gain little beyond low precision, and a few retain substantial error even at low precision. We present TriTile, a training-free attention method that assigns each tile one of three approximation tiers: skipping it by replacing it with its block means, skimming it in NVFP4, or refining it with NVFP4 residual correction. A lightweight router predicts each tile's error under each tier from block statistics and spends extra compute on a tile only where it removes enough error; a single knob, a price on compute, controls the whole speed-quality trade-off. A fused kernel executes all three tiers in a single pass on the FP4 tensor cores. Over dense FlashAttention, TriTile speeds up generation by 1.38-1.83x on Wan2.2 at 23.0-27.6 dB PSNR, 2.28-2.32x on HunyuanVideo at 34.5-36.0 dB, and 1.84x on LTX-2.5 at 34.1 dB, and in every setting it Pareto-dominates every baseline in speed and PSNR.

authors.name: Yeonjae Kim, Omin Kwon, Seong Hoon Seo, Jae W. Lee

papers.title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
papers.summary: Differential privacy requires that algorithms be stable to the change of any record in their input, even to an extreme outlier. Private algorithms thus commonly introduce noise scaled to the worst-case possible influence of any single record. This work studies how to build differentially private algorithms that can effectively tailor their noise to the typical case rather than the worst case. We introduce the general \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR) framework, which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a \emph{typical} record into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on \emph{every} input. We show how to instantiate PFR with a novel filtering step to obtain a general meta-algorithm. Given only a concave friendliness score (which measures how typical a record is with respect to a dataset) and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP (that is, private conditioned on the changed record being typical of the remaining data), it guarantees differential privacy on sufficiently large datasets. The FriendlyCore [TCK+22] and Propose-Test-Release [DL09] algorithms can be viewed as instantiations of our general approach. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation with a dimension-independent sample size, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances in a resistor network, and treatment-rule selection.

authors.name: Moshe Shenfeld, Eliad Tsfadia, Katrina Ligett

papers.title: Quantile Propagation Planning for Budgeted Tail-Risk Evaluation
papers.summary: Risk-aware planning must identify rare, costly outcomes using only a limited number of model evaluations. Monte Carlo rollouts spend this budget on noisy tail estimates, while planning from the mean can miss the tail entirely. We introduce quantile propagation planning (QPP), which propagates a small, fixed set of disturbance quantiles through the dynamics and integrates the resulting cost curve to evaluate both mean and tail risk. The method is exact at the propagated levels, converges as the quantile grid is refined, and admits a one-sided conservatism guarantee under stated structural conditions. In controlled overload and inventory tasks, QPP reduces realized tail cost and constraint violations relative to mean-rollout planning. On overload, it remains competitive with sampled evaluators that use substantially more trajectories. These results position QPP as a transparent, budget-controlled approach to tail-risk evaluation.

authors.name: Weijia Han, Zhi Huang, Lisha Qu, Yuanyuan Tan, Jiayue Meng, Wenjun Chen, Liying Liang, Bangjie Deng

papers.title: ISBC: Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding of Pretrained Text Embeddings
papers.summary: Pretrained text embeddings encode semantic structure in high-dimensional continuous spaces whose coordinates are difficult to interpret. We introduce Interpretable Sparse Binary Coding (ISBC), which learns a small set of binary dimensions from frozen embeddings without taxonomy labels or downstream outcomes. A trainable encoder and affine decoder combine reconstruction with controls on activity, factor utilization, dependence, and activation uncertainty. Individual bits and their conjunctions select overlapping document groups; complete activation profiles provide finer contexts for conditional comparisons. We evaluate these representations across corpora, backbones, and code configurations through reconstruction, geometry, predictive probes, and document inspection. Empirical cases identify both distinctions within existing categories and shared content across their boundaries. In a mixed-domain corpus, the most frequent profiles predominantly identify source collections, while selected within-source comparisons reveal sentiment and migration contrasts. Selected associations persist in additional documents encoded without refitting. In an engagement application, bits alone improve prediction of log-transformed outcomes over a constant reference, while their combinations identify within-event content contrasts associated with engagement. The results support using binary coordinates and their combinations for empirical interpretation, with complete profiles providing a fine, partly initialization-dependent description rather than a unique discrete taxonomy.

authors.name: Stefano Maria Iacus, Haodong Qi

papers.title: Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share
papers.summary: Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example's statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example's patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

authors.name: Amin Najafgholizadeh, Mohsen Afsharchi

papers.title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
papers.summary: Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective. We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.

authors.name: Yi Zhang, Zhixin Zhao, Weiwei Sun, Yitao Hu, Sheng Chen, Keqiu Li

papers.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
papers.summary: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

authors.name: Chaoyun Zhang, Bingxuan Li, Pinxue Guo, Yangfan Gao, Zikun Cai, Tianci Xie, Hui Li, Yuqi Huang, Yifei Cao, Bo Mao, Tian Tang, Qichang Zheng, Tongtong Liu, Xiaoxing Wang, Jinxiu Liu, Lizhi Lin, Zhou Shao, Maosen Zhou, Miao Zheng, Shuo Zhang, Yangji He, Kepeng Lei, Ning Zhao, Wei Shen, Zhenjiang Jin, Xinyue Zhang, Peng Sun, Zhenhua Han, Rui Zheng, Hang Yan

papers.title: Beyond Unit-Circle Eigenvalues: Invariant Bases for Stable State Space Dynamics
papers.summary: Diagonal state space models process long sequences at linear cost, yet the same transition is applied at every step of a rollout, so an unconstrained recurrence holds no quantity fixed and the state decays or grows without bound. Current designs constrain one quantity, and preserving one does not guarantee preservation of the others, so a model can hold its norm to machine precision while momentum drifts by hundreds of percent. We claim that the conserved quantities of a diagonal recurrence are layered, that each layer requires a strictly stronger condition on the operator, and that a unit-modulus spectrum reaches only the outermost. Acting on the claim, we enforce the conditions required for every layer by construction. The generator of the Kronecker-Cayley transition (KC) is a graph Laplacian over object subspaces, $\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{L}\otimes I_m$, advanced by a Cayley transform, and the step stays diagonal at $O(N^3+N^2m)$ cost. The conserved set is exactly a $2m^2$-dimensional family of quadratic forms, held at every parameter value, so the quantities and the dynamics the construction reaches are fixed before training. On four conservation benchmarks, KC holds total mass at or near the reference floor while every diagonal baseline loses it by orders of magnitude. We further compare against mass correction and find that two correctors fail once the underlying prediction diverges, which shows that assembly rather than correction is necessary for a guarantee that holds across the rollout. A free modal basis trained under a conservation penalty conserves only by freezing its spectrum, whereas the assembled operator conserves with every mode but one free to rotate. Beyond these benchmarks, KC holds the linear momentum of three $N$-body systems and, at the operator level, the conserved quantity in molecular dynamics, chemical kinetics, pharmacokinetics and power-grid swing dynamics.

authors.name: Jiaqian Zhu, Yang Zhang, Junhua Ding, Xiaowei Yu

papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.summary: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

authors.name: Farnoush Rezaei Jafari, Tristan Lazard, Kenza Bouzid, Shruthi Bannur, Jeremiah Wander, Ashley Mae Conard, Stephanie Hyland, Lorin Crawford, Daniel Coelho de Castro

papers.title: Replay for LLM Continual Learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain experts into one student and is used in the post-training of recent large language models. It trains on all domains at once, so every expert must be available at the same time. In practice, capabilities often arrive one after another, and the experts of earlier domains may be gone when a new domain is learned. Distilling the experts in sequence then suffers from catastrophic forgetting of the earlier domains. Some recent pipelines store a snapshot after every stage and end with a multi-teacher recovery stage taught by all snapshots. The number of stored models then grows with the number of stages. Different from these pipelines, this paper formulates continual MOPD by what is kept from earlier stages and studies replay toward the previous student. Inside every stage, prompts of earlier domains are replayed with the student of the previous stage as their teacher, so neither earlier experts nor stage snapshots are kept. Two design choices of replay are explored. The replay budget of a stage is either shared among the earlier domains or fixed per earlier domain.
