papers.title: The Environment of High-Energy Transient Host Galaxies at High Redshifts as Observed by SHARP
papers.summary: The study of transient events, such as Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) and extreme Supernovae (SNe), provides a unique probe of star-forming environments in the early Universe. Traditional global host galaxy studies often fail to capture the local conditions around the progenitor, leading to potential mischaracterizations due to metallicity gradients and spatial inhomogeneities. Using high spatial resolution integral field unit (IFU) data, such as those obtained with SHARP/VESPER, allows us to spatially resolve the host galaxies and accurately determine the physical properties (metallicity, stellar age, kinematics) at the precise explosion site. Here, we review the need for near-infrared spatially-resolved observations to link progenitor properties, such as the required low metallicity for long GRBs, to their birth environments, and highlight the crucial role of instruments like SHARP in advancing high-redshift transient science, including the characterization of SNe without associated GRBs and Kilonovae hosts.

authors.name: L. Izzo

papers.title: Net Cooling Tables for Cosmological Simulations under Multiple UV/X-ray Background Models
papers.summary: We present three sets of net cooling tables for cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, computed with CLOUDY 23.01 for optically thin gas in photoionization equilibrium with three different UV/X-ray background models. Following the element-by-element approach, and in a format compatible with existing tables, we tabulate cooling, heating, and net rates separately for hydrogen and helium over an extended range of helium mass fractions and for 13 heavy elements, together with hydrogen species fractions, electron abundances, and mean particle masses. For gas of Solar composition, the choice of UV/X-ray background has little impact on the net cooling rates at low redshift, but the results increasingly diverge towards high redshift, particularly in diffuse gas near thermal equilibrium. Compared with widely used previous tables, cooling times in this regime differ by up to an order of magnitude at $z \gtrsim 4.6$, and the calculations disagree on whether the gas undergoes net cooling or heating over nearly 10% of the diffuse density-temperature plane at $z \approx 8$, corresponding to the intergalactic medium. These trends persist for gas composed exclusively of hydrogen and helium. The tables provide a consistent framework for assessing the impact of the radiation background on gas cooling in cosmological simulations.

authors.name: Laura Di Federico, Klaus Dolag, Ildar Khabibullin, Luca Sala, Geray S. Karademir, Milena Valentini

papers.title: AGN Host Galaxies in COSMOS-Web: Linking Structural Evolution and Star Formation Quenching up to $z=5$
papers.summary: The role of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the suppression of star formation and structural evolution of galaxies during their transition from star-forming to quiescent systems remains unclear. We analyze 3,955 AGNs selected through five multiwavelength diagnostics at $010^{10.5}$) generally exhibit sizes comparable to those of SFGs despite suppressed star formation. Toward lower redshifts, they increasingly approach the QG size-mass relation, accompanied by declining specific star formation rates (sSFRs) and increasing S\'ersic indices. In contrast, lower-mass AGN hosts remain close to the SFG relation across the redshift range. Overall, AGN hosts exhibit relatively mild size evolution, following $R_e\propto(1+z)^{-0.6}$ over $02.2$, however, some AGN hosts exhibit suppressed star formation while retaining relatively extended structures. These findings suggest that some AGN hosts may follow alternative evolutionary pathways in which star formation suppression precedes substantial structural compaction.

authors.name: Xiao Han, Lilan Yang, T. Kelly, Matthew A. Malkan, Luis C. Ho, John D. Silverman, Zi-Jian Li, Andreas L. Faisst, Andrew J. Battisti, Jeyhan S. Kartaltepe, Lauro Moscardini, Rasha M. Samir, Ronaldo Laishram, Tao Wang, Yiyang Zhang, Caitlin M. Casey, Henry Joy McCracken, Jason Rhodes, Brant E. Robertson, Maximilien Franco, Daizhong Liu, Marko Shuntov, Xuheng Ding

papers.title: Gaia DR3 Reveals the Kinematics of Young Stellar Objects in the Carina Nebula: Peripheral Expansion and Central Rotation
papers.summary: We investigate the kinematics of the Carina Nebula using a sample of young stellar objects (YSOs) cross-matched with Gaia DR3, together with $^{12}\mathrm{CO}\,(1\mbox{--}0)$ molecular gas observations and APOGEE radial-velocity data. The results show that the proper motions of the YSOs in the four peripheral subregions of Carina display a systematic outward expansion, and that the two-dimensional expansion velocities of the subregions are approximately $0.57\mbox{--}4.56~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. The YSOs in the Central Region exhibit ordered rotation around an axis at a position angle of $86.9\pm1.5^\circ$, with a rotation velocity of $1.75\pm0.03~\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Further momentum estimates suggest that the current expansion in the peripheral regions may result from the combined effects of feedback from massive OB stars and possible past supernova explosions. These results indicate that feedback from massive stars plays a dominant role in the dynamical evolution of the giant molecular cloud in the Carina Nebula.

authors.name: Xinyu Yang, Yuxin He, Chaojie Hao, Yiwei Dong, Y. Xu, Yingjie Li, ZeHao Lin, DeJian Liu, Jarken Esimbek, Jianjun Zhou, Gang Wu, Xindi Tang, Dalei Li

papers.title: Primary and Secondary Star Formation in the Spiral Waves of NGC 628
papers.summary: To determine the role of spiral arms and stellar feedback on the formation of stars, we examine the positions of optically identified and emerging star clusters in NGC 628. We find that the youngest clusters extend further into the spiral arms at small radii than at large radii, as expected when the angular flow rate through a wave-like arm increases with greater distance from corotation. The embedded or emerging star clusters (eYSCs) are identified relative to four distinct morphological features in the 7.7 micron image: spiral arm filaments, spiral arm spurs, spiral interarm feathers, and bubbles. Spiral arm-related eYSCs are presumably first-generation stars made from interstellar gas that was directly compressed by the density wave, while clusters along the rims of bubbles are secondary generations produced by feedback compression. The mass functions of the first and second generations differ: eYSCs in spiral arm filaments extend to significantly higher masses than eYSCs in bubbles. Secondary star formation continues downstream from primary star formation, removing the expected age gradient through the arms. Bubble eYSCs account for approximately one-third of all the emerging cluster mass. The outer arms have a more mixed distribution of spiral- and bubble-related eYSCs than the inner arms, potentially providing a way to distinguish wave and material arms and to find corotation in wave-like arms. Among the 17 most massive clusters with log M(Msun)>4, eight of them are in four tight pairs; in at least one case, the dynamical time for the pair is comparable to the cluster ages.

authors.name: Bruce G. Elmegreen, Sean T. Linden, Kelsey E. Johnson, Angela Adamo, Daniela Calzetti, Varun Bajaj, Giacomo Bortolini, Matteo Correnti, Ana Duarte-Cabral, Kathryn Grasha, Goran Ostlin, Alex Pedrini, Jenna Ryon, Linda J. Smith

papers.title: The dwarf galaxy NGC 185: the flagship of Andromeda's dwarf galaxies for the study of evolved multiple stellar populations
papers.summary: Reaching galaxies at 10-15 Mpc with HST and JWST requires star formation history (SFH) diagnostics that do not rely on the faint main sequence turn-off. We investigate whether horizontal branch (HB), red clump (RC), and red and asymptotic giant branch (RGB, AGB) stars can fill this role for dwarf elliptical galaxies, using NGC 185 as a test case. We use stellar evolution models of low- and intermediate-mass stars as inputs to population synthesis simulations that reproduce the colour distribution and luminosity function of stars in the (mF606W-mF814W, mF814W) diagram. The study of the stars populating the HB is used to derive the distance modulus and reddening, the average mass loss suffered by the stars during the ascending on the RGB and the SFH occurred during the ancient epochs, before 7 Gyr ago. The luminosity function of the RC gives us constraints on the recent SFH (<8 Gyr). The distribution of HB stars yields a reddening E(B-V)=0.20 mag and a distance modulus DM=24.10 mag for NGC 185. The average mass lost by low-mass stars during the RGB phase is 0.22 +- 0.01 Msun. Star formation was concentrated at early epochs, with half of the stars formed more than 11 Gyr ago. The morphology of the HB indicates essentially no metallicity spread among stars older than 8 Gyr, whereas the slope of the RGB suggests that part of the stars younger than 5-6 Gyr are slightly enriched in metals. Once RGB mass loss is adequately constrained, evolved stars can provide a reliable SFH for dwarf elliptical galaxies well beyond the reach of MSTO-based methods. We discuss the implications for more distant systems and the remaining uncertainties in the underlying stellar models.

authors.name: Paolo Ventura, Chiara Ventura, Richard D'Souza, Flavia Dell'Agli, Matteo Correnti, Claudio Gavetti, Marco Tailo, Miriam Di Stefano, Eric Bell

papers.title: Magnetism among the oldest white dwarfs in the solar neighbourhood
papers.summary: We present a new circular polarisation survey of approximately 100 white dwarfs selected as featureless DC stars and combine our measurements with previous observations. Our compilation contains 205 objects, of which 24 show firm circular polarisation detections, while another four show marginal signals that require confirmation. Four magnetic white dwarfs originally classified as DC show polarisation spectra with significant contributions from spectral lines. Depending on the treatment of these objects and of the marginal detections, the inferred fraction of magnetic objects in the DC selected sample lies between approximately 10 and 14%. Among objects without identifiable line contributions, the circular polarisation never exceeds approximately 2%, substantially below the levels observed in some hotter magnetic white dwarfs with prominent spectral features. This is unlikely a symptom of field decay, since in our sample we find no significant evidence for a dependence of magnetic incidence on cooling age, and magnetic fields are detected in stars with cooling ages exceeding 9 Gyr. Instead, strong spectral line opacity provides a natural mechanism for producing much larger polarisation amplitudes than the continuum. In the full sample considered here, the incidence of detectable magnetism increases with stellar mass. Most average-mass magnetic stars for which repeated observations are available show no clear polarimetric variability, whereas variability appears more common among the most massive objects.

authors.name: Stefano Bagnulo, John D. Landstreet

papers.title: Population synthesis of substellar companions surviving common-envelope evolution
papers.summary: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.

authors.name: Nicolas F. Miranda, Alex Mauch-Soriano, Joaquin A. Barraza-Jorquera, Matthias R. Schreiber, Maria Paula Ronco, Felipe Lagos-Vilches

papers.title: Living near filaments: How environment shapes age profiles in low-mass galaxies
papers.summary: U-shaped radial age profiles have recently been reported in low-mass galaxies. This type of profile differs from the usually observed positive radial age gradients of the low-mass regime. We aim to characterise the environment in which low-mass galaxies with U-shaped age profiles are more commonly found. We use the IllustrisTNG-50 hydrodynamical simulations to select a sample of galaxies with stellar masses ranging from $10^9 \, M_\odot$ to $10^{10} \, M_\odot$. Based on their radial age profiles, we classify the sample into galaxies with and without a U-shaped feature. We define a U-shaped profile as one where stellar ages decrease towards a local minimum and subsequently increase, requiring an age contrast of at least 0.4 Gyr on either side of the minimum relative to its value. We find 145 galaxies with U-shaped age profiles ($\sim 11\%$ of the sample). They are mostly central systems ($\sim 72\%$) and $\sim 82\%$ of them reside within low-mass halos ($M_{200} < 10^{12} \, M_\odot$). We also find that galaxies exhibiting this feature are located at large distances from galaxy groups but close to cosmic filaments, with a median distance of $\sim 265$ kpc, whereas those without U-shaped age profiles tend to be located farther away from these structures ($\sim 351$ kpc).

authors.name: Elisa A. Tau, Diego Pallero, Rory Smith, Ra\'ul Baier-Soto, Antonela Monachesi, Silvio Varela-Lavin

papers.title: APOLLO-Timing: Annealed Phase - Orbit Lattice Linking across Observations for Binary Pulsar Timing
papers.summary: Sparse observations of binary pulsars can leave the orbit and the pulse count across observing gaps uncertain. We present APOLLO-Timing, a Bayesian phase-orbit lattice method that fits timing parameters together with integer pulse offsets between observing sessions. PINT checks the candidate connections at fixed pulse numbers. For PSR J1912-1215, a preliminary Keplerian fit to variations in the apparent spin period and its derivative did not phase-connect 96 times of arrival (TOAs) spanning 1438.07 days in 23 sessions. Starting from its position, spin frequency F0, and first time derivative F1 estimated in that fit, with dispersion measure fixed, APOLLO-Timing recovers the orbit and a unique best-supported phase-connected solution without supplied orbital parameters. A repeat full-data blind search recovers the same pulse counts in 914.0 s, including the final fit. Setting the initial F1 to zero in the 17, 18, and 19 session subsets also recovers the reference path. The solution gives Pb = 17.526 days, x = 23.448 light-seconds, e = 2.65e-5, chi-square = 188.01, and a weighted rms residual of 5.08 microseconds. For a pulsar mass of 1.4 solar masses and inclination of 60 degrees, the inferred companion mass is 0.67 solar masses, favoring a CO/ONeMg white dwarf.

authors.name: Y. R. Wen, D. Zhao, N. Wang, J. P. Yuan, W. M. Yan, J. B. Wang, J. T. Bai, Z. H. Chen

papers.title: Investigating the initial conditions of globular clusters via $N$-body simulations: I. half-mass radius and stellar density
papers.summary: Born out of the turbulent, dense gas of the early Universe, globular clusters (GCs) represent a significantly different star-formation mode compared to the local Universe. To quantify the initial cluster conditions, we perform the long-term dynamical evolution of GCs using the high-precision direct N-body simulation code PeTar. As the first step in a series of studies, we investigate the two low-mass outer-halo GCs, Eridanus and Whiting 1. By comparing simulated number density profiles with observations, we derive best-fit initial half-mass radii of $2.0 \pm 1.0$ pc for Eridanus and $2.5 \pm 0.5$ pc for Whiting 1, corresponding to initial surface densities of $2592.03 M_\odot pc^{-2}$ and $226.35 M_\odot pc^{-2}$, respectively -- 2-3 orders of magnitude higher than their present-day values. The absence of multiple populations (MPs) in Whiting 1 and young massive clusters (YMCs), in contrast to the MP-hosting Eridanus, supports the scenario that MP formation requires higher initial surface density and/or lower metallicity. Using the simulations as a template, we identify five high-probability extra-tidal candidates of Whiting 1 from Gaia DR3 and APOGEE DR17, which exhibit coherent kinematics and chemical abundances. Our results demonstrate that the diffuse states of low-mass GCs are the product of long-term dynamical expansion and tidal stripping, and that their primordial configurations were significantly denser.

authors.name: Ruoyun Huang, Baitian Tang, Long Wang, Holger Baumgardt, Xia Li, Genhao Liu, Jundan Nie, Hao Tian

papers.title: The formation and evolution of Wolf-Rayet stars with temperature-dependent winds
papers.summary: Massive stars strongly influence their environments through their radiation, stellar winds and core-collapse supernovae, while their own evolution is strongly shaped by wind mass loss. Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars are characterised by strong, optically thick winds, and the implementation of these winds remains an important uncertainty in stellar evolution models. Recent hydrodynamically consistent atmosphere calculations predict WR mass-loss rates that depend strongly on the temperature at the wind-launching region. We investigate the effects of incorporating these latest theoretical WR wind prescriptions into single and binary stellar evolution models at Milky Way, Large Magellanic Cloud and Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) metallicities. We find that the temperature dependence of the WR wind can significantly alter the evolution of stars near the threshold for WR formation. In particular, an implementation that transitions from a hydrogen rich WNL wind prescription to a classical WR wind driven by the hot iron opacity bump causes some SMC-metallicity models to spend an extended period at temperatures of approximately 70 to 90 kK. This produces a concentration of models in the temperature range occupied by most observed SMC WR stars, a feature that has previously been difficult to explain with stellar evolution models. Our results demonstrate that incorporating physically motivated, temperature dependent WR winds can improve the agreement between stellar evolution models and observed WR populations.

authors.name: Guy O. Flint, Avishai Gilkis, Tomer Shenar, Christopher A. Tout

papers.title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Refining the strong lens sample with Space Warps crowd-sourced science
papers.summary: We demonstrate the efficacy of crowd-sourced refinement of strong gravitational lens candidate samples by citizen scientists. Binary (lens/non-lens) classification by citizen scientists has been conducted previously, and here we extend such categorisation into `definite', `probable', `possible', and `non-lenses'. This grading is a required stage ahead of any strong lens sample publication and is usually carried out by (small) teams of researchers. We compare the responses of the volunteers to those of strong lens researchers and discuss the optimal strategy for lens classification and grading in future strong lens searches. Volunteers are found to be able to correctly identify systems of each grade, and their responses can be calibrated to be comparable to those of researchers. Grade posteriors, defined as the probability that a strong lens system classified by the volunteers is a certain grade, converge most rapidly for non-lens systems. We find that one researcher classification is equivalent to only 1.9 volunteer classifications when grading such systems. There is significant disagreement in the grading of intermediate-grade lens candidates amongst both volunteers and researchers. Moving towards calibrated lens probabilities for future lens searches would help to account for such subjectivity. If the Q1 lens search was rerun with volunteers performing lens grading (and corresponding calibration), a completeness of 79% for Grades A+B (corresponding to definite + probable lenses respectively) could be achieved with 41% purity prior to researcher inspection - this would correspond to an expected 12500 true lenses (i.e. excluding contaminants) in Euclid DR1.

papers.title: Adaptive Optics for the Extremely Large Telescope: overcoming Point Spread Function challenges with MORFEO
papers.summary: MORFEO is the multi-conjugate adaptive optics (MCAO) relay for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) of the European Southern Observatory. It combines the adaptive mirrors of the telescope (M4-M5) with two post-focal deformable mirrors to deliver a stable, diffraction-limited point spread function over a field approaching 1'. MORFEO senses the atmosphere using six sodium laser guide stars and up to three natural guide stars distributed across a $\sim$160'' technical field, enabling sky coverage levels of order 50% at the South Galactic Pole. Through its two gravity-invariant ports, MORFEO feeds the MICADO first-light imager and spectrograph with a corrected field of 51''and HARMONI, the high-angular resolution integral field spectrograph. SHARP, a concept for a multi-object near-infrared spectrograph at the ELT, adopts MORFEO as its reference MCAO architecture for evaluating achievable image quality and scientific performance. In this paper, we summarise the MCAO capabilities delivered by MORFEO, its optical quality, tomographic performance, stability of the corrected focal plane, and the accuracy of telemetry-based PSF reconstruction, and discuss their relevance for the development of SHARP and other wide-field spectroscopic concepts at the ELT.

papers.title: Probing Solar-Wind Structure During Crab Pulsar Conjunctions with Dispersion and Faraday Rotation
papers.summary: Observations of the Crab pulsar (PSR B0531+21) during solar conjunction probe plasma structure in the inner solar wind through radio-propagation effects. We analyze dispersion measure (DM) and rotation measure (RM) measurements from the annual conjunctions of 2022-2026, obtained with the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME). The 2025 DM time series is distinguished from those of the other years by a secondary enhancement on 21 June, about one week after the main conjunction peak. In our scattering-corrected DM measurements, this feature, $\Delta$DM $= (3.95 \pm 0.20) \times 10^{-3}$ pc cm$^{-3}$, is about 20 times the day-to-day DM scatter outside the conjunction window. The RM time series, measured by combining the single pulses of each observation and corrected for the ionospheric contribution, show conjunction excursions of up to $\sim 60$ rad m$^{-2}$ and changes of sign consistent with crossings of heliospheric magnetic-sector boundaries, but no counterpart to the secondary 2025 DM feature or to a similar post-conjunction DM tail in 2026. From the slope of the RM excess against the DM excess we estimate the electron-density-weighted line-of-sight magnetic field; for the sectors with significant slopes, $|\langle B_\parallel \rangle|$ is at least $\sim 0.2$ to $\sim 10$ mG near conjunction, largest in 2025.

authors.name: Huiyu Xiao, Daniel Baker, Thierry Serafin Nadeau, Hao Shen, Dongzi Li, Ue-Li Pen

papers.title: Can Magnetic Reconnection Accelerate Energetic Particles in the Heliosheath?
papers.summary: The mechanism for accelerating energetic particles in the outer heliosphere is still under debate. The termination shock, turbulence, and magnetic reconnection have all been proposed as viable mechanisms. We investigate compression-driven particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection in the heliospheric current sheet using the MHD--SDE framework that incorporates energetic-particle feedback into the MHD evolution. For the heliosheath conditions considered here, we find that reconnection-driven acceleration is inefficient downstream of the termination shock, whereas reconnection near the heliopause can generate stronger compression and produce a power-law differential intensity spectrum $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-5.4}$. However, even the hardest spectrum achieved during magnetic reconnection remains much steeper than the typical $J(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-1.5}$ spectrum observed in the heliosheath. This indicates that magnetic reconnection alone is insufficient to explain the acceleration of energetic particles in the heliosheath.

authors.name: Jeongbhin Seo, Teresa Boland, Fan Guo, Xiaocan Li, Giulia Murtas

papers.title: Energetic Nonthermal Electrons within the Above-the-looptop Regions in Solar Flares: Acceleration, Feedback, and Quasi-Periodic Pulsations
papers.summary: Solar flares are among the most dramatic events in the solar system, releasing substantial magnetic energy and accelerating a large number of electrons to high energies. Notably, in certain events, the above-the-looptop region may contain a significant population of nonthermal electrons, both in number and energy. For the first time, we adopt a novel numerical method that combines magnetohydrodynamics with energetic particles incorporating feedback from nonthermal electrons to investigate electron acceleration and transport in solar flares. We find that a large fraction of energetic electrons are accelerated via the current sheet and termination shock regions. Most energetic electrons are concentrated in the above-the-looptop region, carrying a sizable amount of the released energy. We observe that greater feedback of nonthermal electrons leads to steeper energy spectra. The energy density of the nonthermal electrons oscillates due to the periodic impact of magnetic islands into the above-the-looptop, which may help explain the observed quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs). Our simulations provide new insights into the origin of nonthermal electrons and associated emissions in the above-the-looptop region.

authors.name: Jeongbhin Seo, Fan Guo, Xiaocan Li, Bin Chen, Chengcai Shen, Hui Li

papers.title: Migration and eccentricity damping timescales in overstable resonant planetary systems: hydrodynamic and N-body simulations
papers.summary: Tidal interactions between planets and discs modify semimajor axes and eccentricities. These effects are represented by migration and eccentricity damping timescales in analytical and Nbody models, although they are assumed constant. This approximation is uncertain in resonant multiplanet systems, where coupled planet disc evolution can produce non-linear torque feedback. We investigate migration and eccentricity damping in two planet systems undergoing resonant and overstable evolution near the 2:1 mean motion resonance. Using hydrodynamic simulations with varying disc surface densities, viscosities, and aspect ratios, we measure both timescales from energy and angular momentum exchange between the planets and disc. We find that both timescales are time dependent and vary throughout the evolution. In resonant systems, sign reversals occur owing to eccentricity oscillations and disc torque variations. Moreover, migration timescales normalised by their expected dependence on planetary mass, disc surface density, and aspect ratio deviate between models. Likewise, the common relation between migration and eccentricity damping timescales is not recovered. We compare the hydrodynamic evolution with several Nbody approaches. Models with constant migration and damping timescales fail to reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution, whereas torque-based approaches provide better agreement. In particular, approaches including corotation torque saturation and planetary eccentricity reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution in the type I migration regime, whereas additional corrections are required when planets partially open gaps. These results show that time-dependent torque-based prescriptions provide a consistent physical link between hydrodynamic simulations and simplified Nbody models of resonant planetary systems.

authors.name: Zahra Afkanpour, Sareh Ataiee, Anna B. T. Penzlin, Alexandros Ziampras, Hadiseh Nabavinezhad, Christoph Sch\"afer, Hilke Schlichting, Rafael Sfair

papers.title: Constraining the white-dwarf mass in the intermediate polar IGR J17014-4306 using X-ray and optical spectroscopy
papers.summary: Intermediate polars (IPs), a subclass of magnetic cataclysmic variables, often show discrepancies between white-dwarf (WD) mass measurements from X-ray spectral modeling and optical dynamical studies. We investigate the IP IGR J17014-4306. We performed a joint spectral analysis of NuSTAR observations combined with archival XMM-Newton and Swift data, modeling the broad-band X-ray spectrum with a multi-temperature cooling-flow model. Additionally, we obtained time-resolved optical spectroscopy with the SOAR telescope to measure the radial velocity of the donor star and constrain the system's orbital parameters. The X-ray spectral analysis reveals a very high post-shock plasma temperature of $kT_{\max}=50_{-8}^{+11}\,\mathrm{keV}$, corresponding to a WD mass of $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.94_{-0.07}^{+0.09}\,M_\odot$. We also fitted the NuSTAR spectrum above 10 keV with the ipolar30KK model, obtaining $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.88_{-0.12}^{+0.14}\,M_\odot$. Our optical spectroscopy yields a radial-velocity semi-amplitude for the companion star of $K_2=165\pm4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and an optical mass function of $f(M)=0.249\pm0.018\,M_\odot$. Combined with the eclipse geometry and the WD mass estimate from the X-ray models, these results favor a high mass ratio, $0.76\lesssim q\lesssim0.95$, and a donor-star mass of approximately $0.67\lesssim M_2/M_\odot\lesssim0.89$. In the limiting case of $q=1$, the WD mass has an upper limit of $1.14\,M_\odot$. Together with the X-ray measurements, this indicates a relatively massive WD. The lack of an independent measurement of the WD dynamical mass leaves it unclear whether the dynamical mass is consistent with the X-ray measurements or whether the X-ray mass is underestimated, as has been found for other IPs. Thus, our constraints make IGR J17014-4306 an important system for improving our understanding of IPs.

authors.name: D. C. Souza, M. P. Diaz, A. S. Oliveira, G. J. M. Luna, C. V. Rodrigues, M. Reynolds, N. Palivanas, I. J. Lima, J. Miko{\l}ajewska, M. Orio

papers.title: Cosmological Backreaction and the Separate Universe Conjecture: Dynamical volume partitioning of Newtonian cosmologies
papers.summary: We provide a description of general Newtonian cosmologies for collisionless matter in terms of an exact and dynamical volume partitioning of global realizations of Newtonian models. Employing the formalism for the description of cosmological backreaction, an interaction between the inhomogeneities of the formation of structures in the Universe and their average properties can be analyzed. Our results can be regarded as a tool for many potential applications in the context of Newtonian simulations, but they also provide an exact way to assume analytical properties of the universe models on regional scales in conformity with global integral constraints on their average properties. We discuss approaches in relation to `separate Universe conjectures' in the literature and examine their consistency with the exact partitioning framework. In particular, using the Average Expansion Rate Approximation (AvERA) as an example, we show that identifying locally assigned Friedmannian rates with physical regional expansion rates is constrained by the global Newtonian 3-torus condition. Alternatively, when the simulation cells are interpreted as non-material control volumes, Reynolds transport introduces mass flux and flux-backreaction terms, so that their dynamics is not in general that of independent Friedmann domains. We also discuss the corresponding consistency conditions for stable clustering prescriptions.

authors.name: Thomas Buchert, Jan J. Ostrowski, Alfred Bovon

papers.title: Magnetic Properties of Galactic Molecular Clouds
papers.summary: The earliest studies of molecular clouds (MCs) showed scaling relations between mass and radius M$\sim$R^s with exponent s $\approx$ 2, known as the third Larson relation. More recent CO surveys indicate 2 < s < 3 in the inner Milky Way (MW) and nearby galaxies. These observations appear consistent with the virial equilibrium (VE) of magnetically subcritical clouds, bound by the pressure Pe of the midplane ISM. The VE equations for such clouds are consistent with 2 < s < 3 for magnetically subcritical clouds, but not for magnetically critical, supercritical, or nonmagnetic clouds. We fit the subcritical VE equations to M-R trends observed in CO surveys of $\sim$1500 clouds, with correlation coefficients 0.8 - 1. The fits indicate median mass-to-flux ratio lambda $\approx$ 0.7, magnetic field strength Btot $\approx$ 60$\mathrm{\mu G}$, and Pe/k $\approx$ 5 x 10^5 cm^-3 K in the inner MW, with lesser values in M33 and M31. For 18 MW "bones," VE analysis assuming likely values of Pe also indicates subcritical values of lambda, as found from polarization observations. These results indicate that many giant molecular clouds (GMCs) are consistent with pressure-bound magnetically subcritical virial equilibrium. If so, GMCs may have low star formation efficiency (SFE) because their relatively strong fields cause filaments, clumps and cores to form slowly, while feedback and turbulence disperse them rapidly. The fields in their clumps and cores are likely weak enough to allow star-forming collapse, according to Zeeman and DCF observations, and according to MHD simulations which predict SFE $\approx$ 0.5-2%.

authors.name: Philip C. Myers (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard and Smithsonian), Ian W. Stephens (Worcester State University), Simon Coud\'e (National Observatory of Japan), Nicole Karnath (Space Science Institute), Howard A. Smith (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard and Smithsonian)

papers.title: Magnetohydrodynamics During Reheating
papers.summary: Reheating is a crucial phase that connects inflation with the hot Big Bang Universe. During this phase, the nonlinear interactions among the inflaton, the radiation plasma, and the primordial magnetic fields can influence the subsequent evolution of cosmic structures we observe today. In this paper, we develop a multifluid framework to investigate the evolution of three dimensional nonlinear magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) during the non instantaneous reheating phase driven by the perturbative decay of the inflaton into the radiation plasma. For the present paper, we consider the simplest scenario where the inflaton field homogeneously injects energy into the radiation sector. We study the MHD evolution of the coupled inflaton radiation system during the reheating phase, including the evolution of their individual kinetic energies, the velocity perturbations, vorticity, magnetic fields, and gravitational waves. We find that homogeneous energy transfer from the inflaton to the radiation sector increases the radiation and kinetic energy densities but does not significantly amplify the initial magnetic field perturbations. Consequently, the magnetic spectrum remains largely unchanged with respect to the instantaneous reheating scenario, while the velocity perturbations undergo a scale redistribution that affects the resulting GW spectrum. Our results demonstrate the importance of nonlinear multifluid MHD dynamics in understanding the evolution of primordial fields during reheating and provide a framework for exploring more realistic scenarios involving inhomogeneous decay processes and detailed thermalization effects.

authors.name: Sovan Sau, Subhasis Maiti, Sahel Dey, Alberto Roper Pol, Debaprasad Maity

papers.title: Tracking turbulence for wind-driven halo removal using MagAO-X pyramid wavefront sensor images
papers.summary: The wind-driven halo (WDH) is a persistent, low spatial frequency noise artifact that arises due to the servo-lag error inherent to all adaptive optics (AO) instruments. Spatial filtering may be employed to overcome this artifact, however, filtering out the WDH while simultaneously preserving signal from an extended astrophysical object of interest is exceptionally challenging. Additionally, since the WDH changes in intensity and position angle through an observation, data-driven algorithms (e.g., KLIP) that are commonly used to subtract the starlight need to be overly-aggressive to remove both the static and dynamic noise components. Since wavefront sensors (WFSs) continuously track the closed-loop residual wavefront error, WFS telemetry presents the ideal resource for combating this type of noise artifact through postprocessing. Using archival WFS telemetry from MagAO-X, which is the "extreme" AO instrument for the 6.5-meter Magellan-Clay telescope, we demonstrate a novel workflow for WDH reconstruction and removal in individual coronagraphic science images. MagAO-X is equipped with a pyramid WFS capable of recording wavefront telemetry at a high-cadence which is saved during data acquisition. Given this, we detail how our WFS data processing pipeline, windsoCC, cross-correlates the recorded closed-loop wavefront to measure the wind vectors of several turbulent layers of the atmosphere above Las Campanas Observatory. We then make use of the wind parameters learned through windsoCC to reconstruct the WDH footprint by leveraging a parametric model. Notably, we demonstrate a dramatic improvement in object recovery using on-sky MagAO-X images of the disk around HR 4796A at visible wavelengths.

authors.name: Jay K. Kueny, Jared R. Males, Alycia J. Weinberger, Laird M. Close, Joseph D. Long, Joshua Liberman, Sebastiaan Haffert, Eden McEwen, Maggie Y. papers.title: Preparing for the Gaia DR4 Epochalypse: Simulated Epoch Astrometry for Substellar Companion Orbit-Modeling Benchmarks
papers.summary: Gaia's fourth data release (DR4) will provide epoch astrometry for billions of sources, enabling the detection of potentially tens of thousands of substellar companions. We present the epochalypse catalog: Gaia DR4-like epoch astrometry for testing orbit-modeling pipelines on a common set of injected systems with known parameters. Onto each of the $5{,}040{,}328$ main-sequence Gaia stars within $500\,{ \rm pc}$ in the G23H catalog, we inject a zero-, one-, and two-companions system, for $15{,}120{,}984$ systems in total. Companion masses and semimajor axes are drawn log-uniformly over $1\,M_{ \rm Mars}$--$80\,M_{ \rm Jup}$ and $0.03$--$100\,{ \rm au}$, with no occurrence model and no detectability cut, so orbital periods extend well beyond the mission baseline and the companion-free population serves as a matched null. We also flag sub-populations of one- and two-companions systems whose companions are potentially detectable, based on an estimated signal-to-noise ratio that accounts for each star's noise, number of transits, and the suppression of signals with periods longer than the baseline. As a demonstration, we run the kepmodel astrometric periodogram on every system and find that signal detection and period localization decouple beyond the DR4 baseline: long-period companions can produce significant astrometric curvature while their periods, and therefore their masses, remain poorly constrained. Under any companion occurrence model, this population of systems where the orbit is detectable but not characterizable will far outnumber the population with fully characterizable orbits. The epochalypse catalog, its full generation pipeline, and a modeling tutorial are publicly available.

papers.title: ReveaLLAGN 3: Revealing the Infrared Spectral Energy Distributions of Low Luminosity AGN
papers.summary: The spectral energy distributions of active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable information on the emission mechanisms taking place in their inner regions. Here we use the James Webb Space Telescope to study the near and mid-infrared spectral energy distributions of seven nearby low-luminosity active galaxy nuclei from 1.7 to 24 $\mu m$. We cleanly separate the AGN spectrum by performing spatial fits of the two-dimensional images across all wavelengths. We then compare these clean unresolved spectra to aperture-based spectra and show that they effectively remove galaxy contamination. Comparing our infrared measurements to X-ray emission, we find that low-luminosity AGN have enhanced near-infrared emission relative to more luminous AGN, a trend that correlates with radio-loudness, while their mid-infrared-to-X-ray ratios are comparable. A majority of our targets show strong compact silicate emission suggesting the presence of warm dust on parsec scales in these systems. We also quantify the near- and mid-infrared power-law slopes and colors of low-luminosity AGN. In the near-infrared we find AGN of all luminosities have similar spectral slopes and colors, however in the mid-infrared, we find low-luminosity AGN typically have steeper slopes and redder colors than more luminous AGN. Both the strong silicate emission and steep mid-infrared slopes disagree with existing models for low-luminosity AGN spectral energy distributions.

papers.title: Shining LIMelight into the dark: Probing Dark matter - baryon interactions with Line Intensity Mapping
papers.summary: Line-intensity mapping (LIM) is an emerging technique for probing both the astrophysics of galaxy formation and the cosmological evolution of large-scale structure. We investigate, for the first time, its potential as a probe of dark matter-baryon (DM-$b$) interactions using the upcoming Carbon Monoxide Mapping Array Project (COMAP) surveys, COMAP-EoR (Epoch of Reionization) and COMAP-ERA (Expanded Reionization Array). Elastic scattering of dark matter (DM) with baryons, i.e., protons ($p$) and electrons ($e$), exchange momentum and heat with the DM, suppressing structure formation and leaving characteristic signatures in the linear matter power spectrum. These effects propagate to the LIM power spectrum (PS) and voxel intensity distribution (VID). We consider momentum-transfer cross sections $\sigma^{\chi b}_{T,n}=\sigma^{\chi b}_{n}v^n$, with $n=0,-2,$ and $-4$, corresponding to contact, electric dipole-moment-like, and Coulomb-like interactions, respectively. Using Fisher forecasts, we obtain the projected sensitivities to $\sigma^{\chi b}_{n}$ from the PS and VID. Our VID-only forecasts combining the 16 and 30 GHz observed bands yield stronger sensitivities than existing cosmological limits for $n=-2$ and $n=-4$ for sub-GeV DM masses. We also explore the potential of combining the PS and VID to probe these interactions. Our study highlights LIM as a complementary probe of DM models alongside other astrophysical, cosmological, and terrestrial searches.

authors.name: Durba Ghosh, Ranjini Mondol, Ranjan Laha

papers.title: Estimating LuSEE-Night's Sensitivity to C{\alpha} Radio Recombination Lines
papers.summary: Carbon radio recombination lines (CRRLs) arising from the cold neutral medium (CNM) of the interstellar medium are potential foregrounds in the 1-50 MHz band that LuSEE-Night will observe from the lunar far side. CRRLs are sensitive probes of the temperature, density, and radiation field of the CNM, and LuSEE-Night will provide sky-averaged measurements in a poorly explored frequency range. We model CRRLs across this band, accounting for doppler, collisional, and radiation broadening, and we estimate line strengths using two independent methods - fixing either the peak or the frequency-integrated optical depth - applied both uniformly across the sky and with region-dependent values informed by prior low-frequency observations. We simulate LuSEE-Night's expected response to these CRRLs and further convolve the beam-diluted spectra with LuSEE-Night's polyphase-filter-bank spectrometer response, including its zoomed-mode frequency resolution of $\sim$390 Hz, to obtain the expected observed brightness temperature. Using these simulated spectra, we estimate the integration time required to detect individual CRRLs at SNR=5 across the six sky models considered. Required integration times range from as short as 30 hours (in the most optimistic model where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-3}$) to 27.6 years (in the most conservative models where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-4}$). Stacking the 361 simulated C$\alpha$ lines between 10 and 50 MHz reduces the integration time needed for an SNR=5 detection to $\sim$11 minutes and $\sim$151 hours respectively, indicating that LuSEE-Night has realistic chances of making a stacked detection of C$\alpha$ RRLs within a realistic mission lifetime, even under the most conservative optical-depth assumptions.

papers.title: Spacetime Evolution Induced by a Massive Cosmic String in Numerical Relativity
papers.summary: Cosmic strings are one-dimensional topological defects formed during phase transitions in the early universe. ''Massive'' cosmic strings possess a sufficiently large tension to close their transverse space, forming a conical singularity outside the string, as a static gravitational effect. In a dynamical context, such strings are expected to drive topological inflation. In this work, we investigate the spacetime evolution induced by the formation of a massive cosmic string in a radiation-dominated cosmological background, imposing cylindrical symmetry. Using full numerical relativity simulations, we observe that the string core undergoes topological inflation and that its boundary moves inwards superluminally, which causally disconnects the core from the outer universe. Between the core and the asymptotic regions, a nearly matter-dominated decelerating region originates sourced by the oscillating string fields. This region is bounded by a local maximum (''belly'') and local minimum (''throat'') of the circumferential radius, while the throat recedes outwards at about 10% the speed of light. Furthermore, a gravitational wavefront is emitted from the string, characterizing the light cone of the string formation. Even behind the wavefront, the exterior region no longer exhibits a ''conical'' structure. Based on the simulation results, we construct a Penrose diagram, reflecting the causal structure of the entire spacetime.

papers.title: QUIJOTE scientific results -- XVIII. New constraints on the polarization of the Anomalous Microwave Emission in bright Galactic regions: $\rho$\,Ophiuchi, Perseus and W43
papers.summary: This work focuses on the study of the AME, an important emission mechanism between 10 and 60 GHz whose polarization properties are not yet fully understood, and is therefore a potential contaminant for future CMB polarization observations. We use new QUIJOTE-MFI maps 11, 13, 17 and 19 GHz, together with other public ancillary data including WMAP and Planck, to study the polarization properties of the AME in three Galactic regions: rho-Ophiuchi, Perseus and W43. We have obtained the SEDs for those three regions over the frequency range 0.4-3000 GHz, both in intensity and polarization. The intensity SEDs are well described by a combination of free-free emission, thermal dust, AME and CMB anisotropies. In polarization, we extracted the flux densities using all available data between 11 and 353 GHz. We implemented an improved intensity-to-polarization leakage correction that has allowed for the first time to derive reliable polarization constraints well below the 1% level from Planck-LFI data. A frequency stacking of maps in the range 10-60 GHz has allowed us to reduce the statistical noise and to push the upper limits on the AME polarization level. We have obtained upper limits on the AME polarization fraction of order <1% (95% confidence level) for the three regions. In particular we get Pi_AME < 1.1% (at 28.4 GHz), Pi_AME < 1.1% (at 22.8 GHz) and Pi_AME < 0.28% (at 33 GHz) in rho-Ophiuchi, Perseus and W43 respectively. At the QUIJOTE 17 GHz frequency band, we get Pi_AME< 5.1% for rho-Ophiuchi, Pi_AME< 3.5% for Perseus and Pi_AME< 0.85% for W43. Our final upper limits derived using the stacking procedure are Pi_AME < 0.58% for rho-Ophiuchi, Pi_AME < 1.64% for Perseus and Pi_AME < 0.31% for W43. Altogether, these are the most stringent constraints to date on the AME polarization fraction of these three star-forming regions.

papers.title: Wide Area VISTA Extragalactic Survey (WAVES): Redshift-limited selection of targets for the Wide survey using decision-tree classification
papers.summary: The Wide-Area VISTA Extragalactic Survey (WAVES) on the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST) includes two flux-limited subsurveys with very high (95%) completeness requirements: Wide over $\sim\!1200$ deg$^2$ and Deep over $\sim\!65$ deg$^2$. Both are $Z$-band selected, and additionally redshift-limited, while the true redshifts are not known a priori but will only be measured by 4MOST. Here, we present a classification-based method to select the targets for WAVES-Wide. Rather than estimating individual redshifts for the input photometric galaxies, we assign probabilities of them being below $z=0.2$, the redshift limit of the subsurvey. This is done with the supervised machine learning approach of eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), trained and tested on a comprehensive spectroscopic sample overlapping with WAVES fields and using nine-band VST+VISTA photometry for the feature space. We check the performance of our classifier both for the fiducial WAVES-Wide limits, as well as for a range of neighboring redshift and magnitude thresholds, finding purity and completeness at the level of 90-95% depending on the test set. The metrics deteriorate for sources close to the selection limits and for test sets selected from DESI, not used in training. We apply the classifier trained on the full spectroscopic sample to the 8.6 million galaxies from the WAVES photometric catalog. This gives us about 1.2 million target candidates, reducing to 1 million if we apply an XGB probability threshold $P_\mathrm{XGB}(z\leq0.2) > 0.72$. Our work demonstrates that a machine-learning classifier could be used to select a flux- and redshift-limited sample from deep photometric data.

authors.name: G. Kaur, M. Bilicki, S. Bellstedt, E. Tempel, W. A. Hellwing, I. Baldry, B. Bandi, S. Barsanti, S. Driver, N. Guerra-Varas, B. Holwerda, C. Lagos, J. Loveday, A. Robotham

papers.title: Euclid: Modelling observational effects in cluster counts and cluster clustering
papers.summary: This study explores the impact of observational and modelling systematic effects on cluster number counts and cluster clustering and provides model prescriptions for their joint analysis in the context of the Euclid survey. Using 1000 Euclid-like cluster catalogues, we investigated the effect of systematic uncertainties on cluster summary statistics and their auto- and cross-covariance, and performed a likelihood analysis to evaluate their impact on cosmological constraints, with a focus on the matter density parameter, $\Omega_{\rm m}$, and on the power spectrum amplitude, $\sigma_8$. Combining cluster clustering with number counts significantly improves cosmological constraints, with the figure of merit increasing by over 300 % compared to number counts alone. We confirm that the two probes are uncorrelated, and the cosmological constraints derived from their combination are almost insensitive to the cosmology dependence of the covariance. We find that photometric redshift uncertainties broaden cosmological posteriors by 20--30 %, while secondary effects such as redshift-space distortions (RSDs) have a smaller impact on the posteriors -- 5 % for clustering alone, 10 % when combining probes -- but can significantly bias the constraints if neglected. We show that clustering data below $60\,h^{-1}\,$Mpc provides additional constraining power, while scales larger than the acoustic oscillation scale add almost no information on $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_8$ parameters. The RSDs and photo-$z$ uncertainties also influence the number count covariance, with a significant impact of about 15--20 % on the parameter constraints.

papers.title: A Smooth Transition from Giant Planets to Brown Dwarfs from the Radial Occurrence Distribution
papers.summary: Measuring the occurrence rates of celestial objects is a valuable way to study their origins and evolution. Giant planets and brown dwarfs produce large Doppler signatures that are easily detectable by modern instrumentation, and legacy radial velocity (RV) surveys have now achieved full orbital coverage for periods <~30 years. However, the Doppler method's sensitivity to companion minimum mass M_c sin i -- as opposed to true mass M_c -- prevents unambiguous characterization using RVs alone, as purported giant planets may be brown dwarfs or stars on inclined orbits. Here we combined legacy RVs with absolute astrometry to re-fit the orbits of 194 companions from the California Legacy Survey. Around 40% (7/18) of the "brown dwarfs" (M_c sin i = 13-80 M_Jup) we refit had true masses above 80 M_Jup. We incorporated our orbital posteriors and target sensitivity maps into a Poisson likelihood model to calculate occurrence as a function of true companion mass M_c (0.8-80 M_Jup) and separation a (0.3-30 AU). The semi-major axis distributions of objects in this range vary smoothly with mass, with Jupiter analogs favoring an abrupt increase in occurrence near 1 AU and brown dwarfs exhibiting a gradual enhancement at wider separations. Marginalized companion occurrence between 1-10 AU decreases smoothly with mass, with brown dwarfs having the lowest occurrence rate: 1.1 (+0.5, -0.4)%. Jupiter analogs are 10 times as common as brown dwarfs per mass interval in this range, demonstrating that the brown dwarf desert extends to 10 AU. The smooth variation in these distributions disfavors a sharp transition mass between "bottom-up" core accretion and "top-down" gravitational instability formation mechanisms, and rather suggests that these processes may produce companions in overlapping mass ranges.

authors.name: Judah Van Zandt, Greg Gilbert, Steven Giacalone, Erik Petigura, Andrew Howard, Luke Handley

papers.title: The Space-Based Time-Domain Revolution in Astrophysics
papers.summary: Space-based time-domain telescopes such as CoRoT, Kepler/K2 and TESS have profoundly impacted astrophysics over the past two decades. Continuous light curves with high cadence and high photometric precision are now available for millions of sources within our galaxy and beyond. In addition to revolutionizing exoplanet science, the data have enabled breakthroughs ranging from the solar system to stellar interiors, the transient universe, and active galaxies. The key summary points of this review are: (1) Stellar astrophysics has been transformed by the ability to probe the internal structures of stars, test the physics of stellar convection, connect stellar rotation and magnetic activity, and reveal complex variability in young stars. (2) Ages of stellar populations probe the formation history of our Milky Way, and binary star variability enables the detection of "dark" galactic populations such as stellar-mass black holes and neutron stars. (3) Early-time observations of explosive transients provide new insights into the progenitors of supernovae, while the quasi-periodic variability of galaxies probes the physics of accretion processes onto supermassive black holes and the tidal disruption of stars. (4) Observations of solar system objects reveal asteroid compositions through their rotation periods and amplitudes, constrain the cloud structure of ice giants, and allow the discovery of new objects in the outer solar system. (5) Open data policies and software have contributed to remarkable scientific productivity and enabled discoveries by citizen scientists, including new exoplanets and exotic variability in mature Sun-like stars.

authors.name: Daniel Huber

papers.title: Inside the cocoon: a comprehensive explanation of the spectra of Little Red Dots
papers.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a new population of compact galaxies, the `little red dots' (LRDs), whose nature remains unclear. We assemble grating spectra for 53 LRD-like objects and use self-consistent radiative-transfer calculations to show that a supermassive black hole embedded in a dense gas cocoon reproduces the spectra in detail, without requiring a stellar-like photosphere. The near-symmetric, electron-scattering-broadened emission line-shapes can be reproduced by cocoons with comparable inflowing and outflowing mass-fluxes. The same cocoon structure also simultaneously accounts for the continuum shapes, H and He line equivalent widths, and absorption features, and predicts metal-line absorption, X-ray weakness, and muted variability. We predict correlations should exist between Balmer break strength, Balmer line absorption, and scattering line width, and confirm their presence in the observed sample. Typical LRDs have black holes of order $10^{6}$ $\mathrm{M}_\odot$ inside ionised cocoons of tens of $\mathrm{M}_\odot$, likely fed by a much larger cold-gas reservoir.

authors.name: A. Sneppen, D. Watson, J. H. Matthews, G. Nikopoulos, N. Allen, G. Brammer, R. Damgaard, K. E. Heintz, C. Knigge, K. S. Long, V. Rusakov, S. A. Sim, J. Witstok

papers.title: Investigating the Circumnuclear Medium of Tidal Disruption Events with Radio Observations
papers.summary: Tidal disruption events (TDEs) are unique tools for investigating quiescent supermassive black hole (SMBH), accretion physics, and circumnuclear medium (CNM) environments. The CNM density profile is of great astrophysical significance, since it provides key diagnostics for the accretion history of dormant SMBH. TDEs can launch outflows that produce radio emission when propagating into the CNM. The synchrotron radio flux density can be described by a series of power-law segments $F_\nu \propto t^{-\alpha} \nu^{-\beta}$. The closure relation (CR), i.e., the relation between the temporal indices $\alpha$ and the spectral indices $\beta$, are therefore monitoring the CNM density profile. In this work, we first collect 53 TDEs with radio observations to date. We then obtain the predicted CR for arbitrary CNM and different dynamical phases of the outflow, and apply to the radio TDE sample. We constrain the CNM density profile for 26 radio TDEs with good data quality. The results are generally consistent with those estimated with equipatition method, suggesting that CR analysis is efficient in the study of CNM profile for a quiescent SMBH.

authors.name: Chang Zhou, Wei-Hua Lei, Xiangli Lei, Po Ma, Shao-Yu Fu, Zi-Pei Zhu

papers.title: Axionlike dark-matter winds driven by galactic baryon redistribution
papers.summary: We examine solutions of the hydrodynamic equations for dark matter (DM) modeled as a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) with axion-like interaction, forming a spherically symmetric halo in dwarf galaxies. Small perturbations and macroscopic decoherence of the BEC DM are driven by variations in the local gravitational background induced by subgalactic baryonic redistribution. Focusing on the core region of a dwarf galaxy, we analyze three astrophysical scenarios parametrized by observational data for NGC 2366: (i) expansion of a gaseous shell mimicking stellar explosions, (ii) collapse of a shell modeling star formation, and (iii) inward contraction of a stellar cluster driven by dynamical friction within a gaseous environment. Our linearized hydrodynamic simulations reveal that while central DM density variations remain within a subtle 0.01% margin, the induced DM winds are extremely suppressed, reaching velocities of only up to several meters per second. This striking suppression challenges the observational prospect of detecting dark-wind signatures. To address the long-term cumulative impact of multiple baryonic events, we establish a quantum excitation framework with a discrete spectrum under natural Robin boundary conditions. In the inhomogeneous DM halo background, which includes an unstable phase region, the lowest long-wavelength radial mode acts as a false vacuum state, experiencing non-viscous quantum relaxation and decaying over a characteristic lifetime of 68 Myr. This mechanism triggers a universal exponential damping of the system's evolutionary operator, while nonlinear three-mode parametric energy exchange, rather than standard open-continuum Beliaev damping, emerges in the next order of perturbation theory to govern the redistribution of stable quasiparticle excitations.

authors.name: A. V. Nazarenko

papers.title: Accretion-powered flares from black hole-disk collisions in galactic nuclei
papers.summary: Black hole impacts on accretion discs in galactic nuclei can power luminous transients, but predicting their observable signatures is challenging because the post-collision flow is highly time-dependent and inhomogeneous. We present a radiative post-processing framework for relativistic hydrodynamics simulations of black hole-disc collisions. Using physically motivated prescriptions for shock heating, optical depth via an eikonal solver, and photon escape fractions that account for photon trapping and diffusion, we predict light curves and spectral energy distributions over a range of disc densities and collision velocities. Our results indicate that the emission is dominated by the long-lived accretion flow onto the secondary black hole, whose mass supply is highly super-Eddington, rather than by cooling of the unbound ejecta. In the parameter range explored, the luminosity is typically of the order of the Eddington luminosity of the secondary and can reach several times this value, and the emission is generically dominated by soft X-rays. We find that lower velocity collisions produce brighter flares, while the disc surface density mainly controls spectral evolution: low-density discs typically produce $\sim$keV-peaked flares with weak spectral evolution, whereas high-density discs show softer early emission and late-time hardening. A depletion-time estimate calibrated to our results suggests characteristic durations of hours to days for intermediate-mass secondaries, and yields $t_{\rm flare} \propto P_{\rm QPE}$. We discuss implications for QPE-like transients and for the SMBH-binary candidate OJ 287. Our framework does not include radiative feedback on the gas, therefore the luminosities should be interpreted only as baseline estimates of the available power for radiation.

authors.name: Joaquin Pelle, Kyohei Kawaguchi, Masaru Shibata, Alan Tsz-Lok Lam

papers.title: Paschen Jumps in Little Red Dots: Evidence for Nebular Continua
papers.summary: Little red dots (LRDs) are broad-line sources at high redshift that were initially identified by their compact morphologies, red colours, and inflection near the Balmer wavelength. The origin of their optical-to-near-infrared continua is debated, with proposed explanations ranging from direct recombination emission to thermalised blackbodies from stellar-like atmospheres. We report evidence of Paschen jumps in a subset of LRDs with a high signal-to-noise ratio, consistent with free-bound recombination to hydrogen $n=3$. The Paschen and Brackett continuum shapes in the LRD sample are consistent with minimally reddened nebular emission from low-temperature gas with $T_e\lesssim10\,000$ K, while the Paschen jump signatures limits scenarios in which the emission is thermalised. Further, the extreme H$\alpha$ equivalent widths and the tight observed correlation between H$\alpha$ and the continuum follow naturally if both originate in recombination emission. This provides an observational upper limit on the contribution of any direct active galactic nucleus accretion component and any stellar-atmosphere-like component, and also on the fraction of line emission that can be thermalised as it traverses the cocoon. Ultimately, ionised gas emission provide a self-consistent explanation of the continuum, line strengths, and line profiles without requiring multiple separately fitted components.

authors.name: Albert Sneppen, James H. Matthews, Darach Watson, Alex J. Cameron, Stuart A. Sim, Joris Witstok, Gabriel B. Brammer, Kasper E. Heintz, Georgios Nikopoulos

papers.title: Clumps in a Cocoon: Geometry and Mixing Set the Universal X-ray to H$\alpha$ Surface Brightness Ratio
papers.summary: Recent observations reveal a nearly universal X-ray to H$\alpha$ surface-brightness ratio, ${\rm SB}_{\rm X}/{\rm SB}_{\rm H\alpha}\sim 3$, in galactic winds, ram-pressure-stripped tails, and cluster filaments. This is surprising, given the very different temperatures traced by the X-ray and H$\alpha$ emission. Plane-parallel mixing-layer models do not recover this ratio. We run 3D wind-tunnel simulations in the high density-contrast ($\chi\sim 10^3$) regime, where the cold phase shatters into small H$\alpha$-emitting clumps embedded in a volume-filling X-ray cocoon. After smoothing on the tail-width scale, the simulated ratio converges to the observed value. The hot-gas entrainment rate sets the bolometric luminosity, $L_{\rm bol} \propto \dot{M}_{\rm in}$. H$\alpha$ carries a nearly fixed fraction of this luminosity, set mainly by atomic emissivity near $10^4$ K. The X-ray-emitting mass is the same entrainment rate multiplied by the residence time in the X-ray-emitting temperature band, and its luminosity is the corresponding thermal energy divided by the cooling time. Hence $L_{\rm X} \propto \dot M_{\rm in} \propto L_{\rm bol}$, with the X-ray fraction set by the residence-to-cooling-time ratio. An age diagnostic constrains the residence time to be far shorter than the cooling time, making the X-ray and H$\alpha$ fractions comparable. Their common scaling with $L_{\rm bol}$ explains the correlation, while the comparable bolometric fractions explain why the observed ratio is order unity.

authors.name: Zirui Chen, S. Peng Oh, Drummond B. Fielding, Lachlan Lancaster, Yuan Li, Brent Tan

papers.title: MusE GAs FLOw and Wind (MEGAFLOW) XIV: Background-Galaxy Absorption Reveals Kiloparsec-Scale Structure in the Cool Circumgalactic Medium
papers.summary: The properties of the cool ($T\sim10^4$~K) gas in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) are closely linked to the physical mechanisms that create and maintain this multiphase medium. The cool CGM is thought to consist of discrete clouds, whose characteristic size is unknown. Here we present a geometric and direct approach to constrain the coherence scale of these cool structures using stacked MgII absorption lines measured against extended background galaxies and effectively point-like background quasars, whose sizes are a few kpc and $\lesssim 0.01$pc, respectively. When the background-source size is smaller than the coherence scale of the foreground clouds, incomplete covering lowers the detection fraction and causes the median stacked absorption to differ from the mean. For stacked MgII absorption against background galaxies, the mean and median equivalent width (EW) profiles are broadly consistent. For stacked MgII absorption against background quasars, by contrast, the median and mean EW profiles differ significantly, reaching a $\approx10\sigma$ difference beyond 100 kpc. Furthermore, we find that the median and mean EW profiles are broadly consistent for large background galaxies (median half-light radius $\approx 6.6$ kpc), but differ at the $\approx3\sigma$ level for small background galaxies ($\approx 1.5$ kpc). This suggests that the MgII-bearing gas has an effective transverse coherence scale of order a few kiloparsecs, broadly consistent with the $\sim$2--7 kpc range probed by the background galaxies. Using a toy model in which the CGM is populated with discrete cool clouds, we show that the observed differences arise naturally from the combination of partial covering and beam averaging. Our results provide a new geometry-based measure of the small-scale structure of cool CGM gas.

papers.title: IceCube Real-time Searches for High-energy Neutrinos Coincident with LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Gravitational-Wave Alerts in O4a
papers.summary: Gravitational-wave events from mergers of compact objects are a predicted source of high-energy neutrinos. Using data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, we search for neutrinos coincident with 85 significant and 945 low-significance gravitational-wave candidate events from compact binary coalescences published in real-time by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during the first part of its fourth observing run (O4a) and its preceding engineering run, within a time window of $\pm500$ seconds from the merger time. We report improvements to the online pipelines, including automatic sending of notices, which improved the median IceCube real-time response compared to the previous observing run by a factor of 2.7 times faster. In addition, we search for long-duration neutrino emission from three candidate events: two neutron star-black hole mergers and one low-significance gravitational-wave event with a possible subthreshold gamma-ray counterpart. We use two methods, both of which have been previously used to search for neutrinos from gravitational-wave transients: an unbinned maximum likelihood analysis on significant alerts and a Bayesian analysis accounting for astrophysical priors on all alerts. We find no statistically significant emission from any individual gravitational-wave event analyzed. In the unbinned maximum likelihood search, the lowest $p$-value event is S231029y, with $p=0.0079$ ($0.752$ post-trials). In the Bayesian search, the lowest $p$-value for significant events is S230904n, with $p=0.0076$ ($0.9996$ post-trials), and for low-significance events is S231025a, with $p=0.0011$ ($0.678$ post-trials), with an overall population $p$-value of $0.55$. We accordingly set upper limits for each event on the time-integrated flux and energy emitted in neutrinos, assuming isotropic emission.

papers.title: Effect of tidal gravity and planetary rotation on the retrieved atmospheric abundances of close-in exoplanets
papers.summary: Most modern atmospheric retrievals adopt the simplifying assumption that the planetary atmosphere endures no planetary rotation and stellar tidal effect. However, for tidally locked close-in exoplanets, the gravitational influence of the host star and the rapid rotation of the planet can significantly modify the effective gravity, leading to changes in the atmospheric scale height and mixing ratios of molecular abundances. In this work, we develop a combined framework to include these rotation and tidal effects into a forward and retrieval model to study how they affect the molecular abundances of close-in exoplanets. We specifically apply our model to the planet WASP-12b, observed with HST, and WASP-121b, observed with JWST, and investigate how atmospheric retrieval parameters change when tidal and centrifugal corrections to gravity are included. The forward model calculation for strongly affected gravity in WASP-12b shows an increment in transit depth in the range of 300-600 ppm for major molecules, whereas for WASP-121b with relatively less gravity reduction shows variations of 60-140 ppm. The atmospheric retrievals for both planets with and without effective gravity corrections show differences in the retrieved molecular abundances. To validate the detectability of these gravity-induced changes, we perform synthetic injection-recovery experiments over a broad wavelength range, which show statistically significant shifts in the retrieved atmospheric parameters for simple atmospheric compositions, while more complex atmospheric compositions exhibit smaller changes due to increased retrieval degeneracies. Finally, we investigate the robustness of these results using non-isothermal P-T profiles and cloudy atmospheric models, and find that the inferred trends remain qualitatively consistent.

authors.name: K. Arnav, Gopal Hazra

papers.title: Morpho-kinematic of galaxies at cosmic noon
papers.summary: Recent studies of local galaxies highlight the need for high-resolution photometry and kinematics to accurately characterize galactic structures. From this, limitations emerged in the standard two-phase evolutionary scenario, where galaxies first form dispersion-supported bulges followed by secular disk growth. IFS surveys, combining photometry and kinematics, demonstrated that morphology and dynamics correlate weakly, with bulges and disks forming a continuum in their kinematic properties. This scenario is further supported by JWST observations. From analyses based on visual morphology emerged that mature galaxies with distinct morphological features exist at earlier times than expected. This, however, needs to be confirmed with high-resolution stellar kinematics observations. We, therefore, propose to measure stellar kinematics at high spatial resolution for massive galaxies at cosmic noon to probe the build-up of central regions and to disentangle the true nature of structures inferred from visual morphology (e.g., disks and bulges with different degrees of rotation). This will enable studying how galaxy mass, kinematics, and star formation co-evolve, providing a complete census of galactic structures and their formation pathways. In this regard, the VESPER-SHARP instrument on the E-ELT is uniquely suited for this program, offering, within reasonable exposure times, rest-frame optical coverage at $z\sim2$, high spatial resolution, a suitable field of view, and multiplexing for simultaneous observations.

authors.name: F. Rigamonti, F. R. Ditrani

papers.title: SHARP -- A spectrograph proposal to fully exploit ELT capabilities and look beyond JWST
papers.summary: The Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), with their large apertures and cutting-edge Multi-Conjugate Adaptive Optics (MCAO) systems, promise to deliver data that is both sharper and deeper than even the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) across large fields. SHARP is a concept study for a near-IR (0.95-2.45 $\mu$m) spectrograph specifically designed to fully exploit the collecting area and angular resolution capabilities of the upcoming ESO's ELT. The instrument concept is driven by the goal of tackling the most important questions in astrophysics and cosmology, from exploring primordial galaxies to studying the formation of young stellar object and planetary systems in the nearby dust-enshrouded regions, bridging the gap between the local and the distant Universe. This requires versatility to accommodate diverse observational needs. SHARP is composed of two main units: NEXUS, a Multi-Object Spectrograph (MOS) optimized for detecting the faintest sources, and VESPER, a multi-object Integral Field Unit (multi-IFU) designed for brighter ones. This article provides an overview of the scientific design drivers, the solutions developed to meet them, and the resulting optical design that achieves the required performance.

papers.title: A new era for Dual AGN science with SHARP
papers.summary: The search for and the characterization of ultra-compact dual active galactic nuclei (AGN) are among the hottest topics of current extragalactic astrophysics. These systems involve two accreting massive black holes (MBHs) embedded within the same host galaxy, with relative projected separations from a few hundred pc down to a few pc. They are central to understanding hierarchical galaxy formation, black hole growth and demographics, and accretion-feedback coupling in the most extreme interaction phases. Even more compellingly, such tight pairs are the most direct precursors of gravitationally bound binary MBHs (sub-pc scale separation), which are among the loudest emitters of gravitational waves (GWs) in the low-frequency ranges. SHARP will deliver the first statistical census and physical characterization of ultra-compact dual AGN up to cosmic distances, finally bridging the observational gap between kpc-scale pairs and sub-pc GW-emitting binaries, and enabling a breakthrough understanding of MBH growth, feedback and co-evolution across cosmic time.
