papers.summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel instantaneous frequency (IF) estimator for multicomponent signals (MCSs), that takes into account the potential presence of interference in the time-frequency (TF) plane. Our approach optimizes the spectrogram window locally in the TF domain to enhance signal representation, adapting to isolated or interfering modes. This optimization leads to the definition of candidate IF points, which are then gathered together using a novel ridge detection approach, and, finally, IF estimates are obtained by adapting a spline fitting procedure to the potential presence of crossing modes. An extra benefit of the proposed technique is that it also gives access to estimates of the instantaneous amplitudes of the modes, and thus to that of the ideal TF signature of the signal. The proposed IF estimation method compares favorably with state-of-the-art techniques especially on MCSs containing modes with very different frequency modulation.

authors.name: Sylvain Meignen (DAO), K\'evin Polisano (SVH)

papers.title: On the Optimality of Implicit Feedback in Markov Decision Processes over Imperfect Links
papers.summary: Goal-oriented communication protocols are explicitly designed to support the objectives of target applications, such as the monitoring and control of remote processes, while minimizing data traffic. This study considers a transmitter node that observes the environment state and sends it to a remote agent, which then performs control actions. This problem can be modeled as a remote Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a subclass of decentralized POMDPs. Existing studies limit transmissions through communication costs, but neglect the effect of channel impairments and non-ideal or delayed feedback. In this work, we study the optimal joint transmission and control policies over lossy forward channels without explicit acknowledgments. We introduce \emph{revealing} policies, under which the receiver's action, observed directly by the transmitter, discloses the outcome of the forward transmission, keeping the two agents synchronized without a feedback channel. We derive sufficient conditions for the optimality of time-invariant policies in this implicit feedback regime for general POMDPs, along with strictly weaker sufficient conditions in the special case of contextual bandits. Our simulations over a family of remote POMDPs show that these conditions are conservative, and revealing policies are optimal over a substantially wider parameter range than the conditions warrant.

authors.name: Romain Planchon, Federico Chiariotti, Federico Mason, Andrea Zanella, Deniz Gunduz

papers.title: Vision-Aided Near-Field Channel Estimation for XL-MIMO
papers.summary: In wideband extremely large-scale MIMO (XLMIMO) systems, the transmitter (TX) is often in the near field of the base station array. The resulting spherical wavefront makes the line-of-sight channel depend on both the TX angle and distance. Existing polar-domain estimators sample both parameters across the entire coverage region, requiring many candidate positions and pilots. This paper proposes a vision aided framework that uses the object carrying the TX, as seen in a camera image, to restrict the candidate positions to a small grid on that object. An on-grid vision-aided coarse localization (V-CL) algorithm obtains a coarse estimate from the grid points that best fit the received pilots, and an off-grid vision-aided Nelder-Mead refinement (V-NMR) algorithm refines it over continuous angle and distance, from which the channel is reconstructed. Simulations show that the proposed algorithms achieve higher accuracy than both wideband and narrowband polar-domain estimators while requiring far fewer pilots and candidate positions.

authors.name: Sachira Karunasena, Angel Lozano, Tom Drummond, Rajitha Senanayake

papers.title: Spatial Differences Analysis of Nodal Frequency Considering Frequency-Voltage Coupling
papers.summary: The rising penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) brings rich control dynamics that can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency through frequency-voltage (F-V) coupling. Existing analyses often neglect voltage dynamics or only examine the aggregate frequency, leading to overoptimistic evaluation of frequency security. To address these drawbacks, this paper develops a unified model of synchronous generators (SGs), grid-following (GFL)-IBRs, and grid-forming (GFM)-IBRs based on the magnitude and phase dynamics of equivalent internal electromotive force (EMF). Integrating these source models with network equations yields a sparse implicit closed-loop model, which fully captures the device-network F-V coupling without transfer-matrix inversion. Then, the obtained nodal responses are decomposed into common and differential modes. Using this decomposition, coupling indices and pole-residue analysis reveal how F-V coupling can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency and how source configuration and parameters modify this effect. Finally, case studies on the modified IEEE 39-bus and 118-bus test systems validate the proposed model and demonstrate its computational efficiency.

authors.name: Xiaodan Li, Donghai Zhu, Zining Liu, Zhu Guo, Jiabing Hu, Hong Rao

papers.title: Neural Network-based Control Systems with Application to Flight Control, From Classical Neural Control to Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: This book provides a comprehensive and systematic exploration of neural network-based intelligent control systems for aerospace applications, bridging foundational theory with practical implementation. It is structured into two primary parts: Part I covers model-based control design, detailing Feedback Error Learning (FEL), pseudocontrol strategies, and neural backstepping for strict-feedback systems, along with practical refinements such as learning rule modifications, composite learning, and discrete-time formulations, all grounded in rigorous Lyapunov stability analysis. Part II introduces model-free control, laying the groundwork for Reinforcement Learning and Approximate Dynamic Programming. Throughout, theoretical concepts are solidified through detailed case studies on quadrotor UAVs, fixed-wing aircraft (GTM), satellites, and hypersonic flight vehicles, complete with performance metrics, parameter sensitivity analyses, and discussions of actuator faults, input constraints, and wind disturbances, making the book an invaluable resource for students and practicing engineers seeking to design, simulate, and analyze intelligent flight control systems.

authors.name: Seyyed Ali Emami, Paolo Castaldi, Mohammad Narimani, Mahdi Shahrajabian, Mostafa Ezabadi, Alireza Ettelaei, Hosein Saadatmanesh, Zahra Shahbazi

papers.title: PARGAR: Pilot-Aware Graph Attention for Sparse-Pilot Neural OFDM Receivers
papers.summary: Reliable channel estimation and symbol detection in 5G New Radio (NR), as well as emerging 6G radio systems, rely on demodulation reference signals (DMRS). The density and placement of these pilots on the orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) time--frequency resource grid affect both receiver reliability and spectral efficiency. Sparse DMRS layouts increase the time--frequency distance between pilot observations and data resource elements (REs), which can make pilot information harder to exploit with purely local processing. This paper proposes \textbf{PARGAR (Pilot-Aware Graph Attention Receiver)}, a graph-attention neural receiver that represents the OFDM resource grid as a graph for bit detection. The graph combines local time--frequency edges with pilot-anchor links from data REs to selected pilot REs, and we further study a channel-scaled pilot-anchor rule based on approximate coherence time and coherence bandwidth. Using Sionna-generated OFDM simulations, we evaluate \textsc{PARGAR} against DeepRx, a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based receiver, across dense, two-symbol sparse, and single-symbol sparse DMRS layouts under channel-mismatch scenarios. Under the considered SISO uncoded setup, channel-scaled \textsc{PARGAR} explicitly injects pilot-aware inductive bias and yields lower BER in selected sparse-pilot scenarios while remaining competitive under dense pilots.

authors.name: Sajedeh Norouzi, Mostafa Rahmani Ghourtani, Eric Samikwa, Torsten Braun

papers.title: OSD-JSCC: Neural Joint Source-Channel Coding with One-Step Diffusion
papers.summary: Neural joint source-channel coding (JSCC) enables efficient image transmission over noisy channels, yet distortion-optimized approaches often produce blurry reconstructions. While diffusion priors can enhance visual fidelity, their iterative sampling incurs substantial decoding latency. To address this limitation, we propose OSD-JSCC, an SNR-adaptive JSCC framework with a single diffusion step. Specifically, OSD-JSCC transmits pretrained variational autoencoder (VAE) latents through an SNR-conditioned JSCC codec and incorporates two key designs. First, we introduce a stochastic diffusion-state interface that enables the JSCC decoder to predict a Gaussian diffusion state rather than a clean latent, while extracting image-specific semantic tokens. The sampled diffusion state preserves spatial structure and provides a good initialization for one-step refinement, whereas the semantic tokens, together with an SNR token, guide the reconstruction process. Second, we develop SNR-conditioned feature modulation and adaptive timestep selection to jointly adapt latent transmission and diffusion refinement to varying channel conditions. Furthermore, we adopt a three-stage training strategy with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to efficiently adapt the pretrained diffusion prior to the JSCC task. Extensive experiments on Kodak and CLIC2020 demonstrate that OSD-JSCC achieves superior perceptual quality and decoding efficiency. Compared with existing diffusion-based JSCC baselines, OSD-JSCC reduces LPIPS by approximately 43% on Kodak and 53% on CLIC2020, while achieving up to a 50.6$\times$ reduction in decoding latency.

authors.name: Shunpu Tang, Qianqian Yang

papers.title: ARIA: Anti-diagonal Reduced-cost Index-masked Adaptive BLMS Algorithm
papers.summary: The block least-mean-square (BLMS) algorithm supports high-throughput adaptive filtering but incurs high computational cost as the filter length and block size increase. This letter proposes anti-diagonal reduced-cost index-masked (ARIA) adaptive BLMS, which reduces coefficient-update multiplications through anti-diagonal index masking and tap-wise step-size scaling while keeping the filtering exact. Mean-square error (MSE) analysis establishes an explicit step-size bound, and misadjustment. An extension, ARIA-MF (ARIA with masked filtering), also applies the mask during filtering; its analysis shows that the excess MSE is redistributed across block rows while its block average is approximately preserved. Simulations validate the analysis and shows very good agreement with the estimates

authors.name: Mohd Tasleem Khan

papers.title: Adapting Sleep Foundation Models for Dense Sleep Spindle Localization
papers.summary: Adapting sleep foundation models to dense electroencephalography (EEG) event localization is challenging because multi-second representations may not preserve sufficient temporal detail for precise boundary recovery. We address sleep spindle localization by adapting a frozen SleepFM encoder with a local time-frequency pathway that preserves spindle-relevant spectral content and intra-token position. The local representation drives localization, while residual cross-attention incorporates SleepFM temporal context. Dense predictions are obtained through localized token-to-sample reconstruction and temporal refinement. Tested on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA), the proposed model achieves an event-level $F_1$ of $0.8080 \pm 0.0040$ at IoU 0.2 across six folds. Ablations show that localization primarily depends on local spectral and sub-token temporal information, while the pretrained representation provides complementary context. These results indicate that dense adaptation benefits from preserving information below the pretrained token scale. Code will be released upon acceptance.

authors.name: Alexis Bollengier, Abel D\'iaz Berenguer, Olivier Pallanca, Andr\'e Anjos, Hichem Sahli

papers.title: Box-Shift: Fixed-Complexity Counter-Hypothesis Generation for Soft-Output MIMO Box Decoding
papers.summary: Box Decoding is a sort-free tree-search multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detector with a fixed per-layer cost independent of the quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) order. Its regular datapath is well suited to hardware implementation, but the detector has so far been limited to hard-output operation in uncoded systems. Its fixed four-point box spans two adjacent Gray-coded QAM levels per axis, leaving most bits without counter-hypotheses for higher-order QAM. This missing counter-hypothesis (MCH) problem prevents the direct computation of finite max-log log-likelihood ratios (LLRs). We propose the \emph{Box-Shift} algorithm, which shifts the existing box to the nearest node carrying the complementary value of each Gray-coded bit at each detection layer. Unlike Bit-Flip, Box-Shift analytically identifies the partially optimal counter-hypothesis using one inverter per bit and updates the path metric through an index-domain increment. The proposed method preserves the sort-free, QAM-order-independent structure of Box Decoding. Coded $4\times4$ MIMO simulations using 5G~NR low-density parity-check (LDPC) coding show that Box Decoding with Box-Shift achieves a $0.7$--$1.5$\,dB gain in $E_b/N_0$ over the same detector with Bit-Flip at a bit error rate of $10^{-5}$, with equal soft-candidate budgets. For the soft-candidate metrics, the incremental update of Box-Shift needs $75\%$ fewer real multiplications than the explicit evaluation of Bit-Flip at a comparable number of real additions.

authors.name: Shengchun Yang, Amit Sravan Bora, Emil Mat\'u\v{s}, Gerhard Fettweis

papers.title: From Vision to Context: A Review of Prompt-Driven Target Volume Segmentation in Radiotherapy
papers.summary: Accurate target volume (TV) segmentation is essential for radiotherapy (RT) planning but remains time-consuming. Moreover, the final contour depends on the expertise of the radiation oncologist. Although deep learning has improved medical image segmentation, image-only models cannot encode the clinical reasoning that governs TV delineation, particularly for the clinical target volume (CTV), where boundaries are defined by clinical knowledge rather than imaging features alone. Prompt-driven segmentation has recently emerged as a strategy to address this limitation. This work aims to review these approaches for RT TV segmentation with four objectives: (1) compare the different prompting techniques used; (2) compare their performance against image-only baselines; (3) assess how they are evaluated against standard metrics, including the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95th Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, precision, and clinical assessment; and (4) identify the gaps needed for clinical translation. We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and arXiv for studies incorporating geometric, clinical text, or interactive prompts into deep learning models for RT TV delineation. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria, spanning head and neck, breast, prostate, lung, cervix, and rectal cancers. Seven studies used clinical text prompting, four used geometric prompting, and two used interactive prompting; three combined modalities. Reported DSC ranged from 0.67 to 0.93, compared to 0.65 to 0.91 for image-only baselines. None reported sensitivity or precision. Clinical text prompting appears well suited to CTV delineation. Evidence remains limited, and standardized prompt engineering and clinical validation are needed before these approaches can be translated into routine RT practice.

authors.name: Bakpen Kombat, Guus Grimbergen, Maarten L. Terpstra, Gert J. Meijer, Lois, A. Daamen

papers.title: Iteration-Free Candidate Pruning and an Index-Domain VLSI Architecture for Sort-Free MIMO Box Decoding up to 1024-QAM
papers.summary: Wi-Fi~7 and 5G NR use constellations up to $4096$-QAM and $1024$-QAM at multi-gigabit peak rates. The MIMO detector must sustain these rates at a low cost. Linear MMSE detection meets these rates at low cost but loses several dB in SNR. $K$-Best detection recovers this loss, but its per-layer sorting grows with the modulation order and needs large sorting networks or deep pipelines at these rates. Box Decoding is a sort-free tree-search detector whose complexity does not depend on the QAM order, and its deterministic pruning keeps the cost fixed as the MIMO size grows. Single-step candidate pruning (SCP) is fully parallel but less accurate, while iterative candidate pruning (ICP) is more accurate, but its selection loop costs either throughput or area. This paper proposes Max-Min-Exchange Candidate Pruning (MMECP), which replaces the selection loop of ICP with a single max-min exchange without a feedback path and keeps \mbox{near-$K$-Best} performance. The paper also presents a VLSI architecture that represents each candidate by its integer constellation index, so that candidates and their distances are obtained by bit selection instead of operations on symbol values. A $4\times4$ detector synthesized in TSMC $16$\,nm detects one vector per cycle at $1$\,GHz for $64$- to $1024$-QAM and produces up to $40$\,Gb/s, while its gate count grows by $63\%$ over this range. Its normalized hardware efficiency is $2.3\times$, $12\times$ and $14\times$ that of the best compared hard-output detector at $64$-, $256$- and $1024$-QAM.

authors.name: Shengchun Yang, Amit Sravan Bora, Emil Mat\'u\v{s}, Gerhard Fettweis

papers.title: Enhanced Imitation Learning of Model Predictive Control through Importance Weighting
papers.summary: The approximation of model predictive control (MPC) algorithms with neural network models has received significant attention in the power electronics research community, as a valuable tool to enable the real-time implementation of computationally expensive methods. Training machine learning models to imitate MPC algorithms typically follows a traditional supervised learning flow, with a static training data set generated through either uniform sampling or simulation. Training with uniformly distributed data allows models to maintain consistent performance throughout the entire operating space, but very small models may fail to achieve satisfactory results in the regions corresponding to expected operation. Conversely, simulation data can be used in training to obtain models that can accurately track certain trajectories but fail to achieve adequate performance in underrepresented regions. The present article proposes a method to combine the advantages of both methods, by training models on sampled data with importance weights obtained through the kernel density estimation of experimental data. This allows the training process to target specific regions of the operating space, and results in measurable performance improvements. The method is demonstrated through the imitation of a moving discretized control set MPC algorithm for a dual active bridge converter, and is validated through experimental results.

authors.name: Pere Izquierdo G\'omez, Miguel E. L\'opez Gajardo, Nenad Mijatovic, Tomislav Dragicevic

papers.title: Delay-Doppler Synchronization for Distributed Uplink Interference Nulling in LEO Networks
papers.summary: Cooperation among low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provides spatial diversity for mitigating uplink interference that is difficult to suppress with a single onboard array. Coherent interference cancellation across satellites, however, requires compensation of the relative delay and Doppler of a common interferer. We analyze two-branch interference nulling with finite training and derive a closed-form approximation to the mean residual interference-to-noise ratio (INR). The approximation separates wrong acquisition, local synchronization errors, and weight-learning losses, linking performance to input INR, branch power imbalance, training length, and effective search size. Under a Gaussian surrogate with small errors and efficient, approximately unbiased refinement, correct acquisition yields a high-INR plateau of $2/N_v$, where $N_v$ is the valid training length. Synchronization and weight learning contribute equally to this limit, whereas persistent alignment bias adds a penalty that grows with input power. Monte Carlo experiments compare dense FFT/zoom and coarse FFT/gradient acquisition using matched final FIR refinement, branch-noise normalization, and independent test blocks. Both approach the predicted plateau at high input INR. Coarse search reduces measured search time by $6.7\times$ at an approximately 0.7-dB acquisition-threshold penalty. Controlled power-ratio sweeps show how branch imbalance delays reliable acquisition at fixed stronger-branch INR. A separate Starlink snapshot evaluation demonstrates comparable nulling performance under changing satellite geometry.

authors.name: Stefan Daniel Tancovici, Shizhen Jia, Marco Mezzavilla, C. Nicolas Barati, Sundeep Rangan

papers.title: Intra-Cell Spatial Reuse in LEO Downlinks: Beam-Leakage-Aware Satellite Scheduling
papers.summary: Dense low-earth-orbit (LEO) constellations offer an opportunity to increase local broadband capacity by serving multiple terminals in the same cell through concurrent satellite beams. However, interference between overlapping beams limits spatial reuse, and satellite selection based solely on link strength or angular separation may result in suboptimal performance. This paper proposes beam-leakage-aware satellite scheduling for Ku-band LEO downlink transmissions. With matched transmit and receive beamforming, we formulate a fixed-cardinality sum-rate maximization problem that jointly accounts for satellite-dependent received powers and pairwise receive-array leakage. A beam-leakage-aware branch-and-bound (BL-BnB) algorithm combines an admissible upper bound with greedy-plus-swap initialization to obtain globally optimal schedules for the reference-point model. We evaluate the method using a 24-h ephemeris-derived Starlink visibility trace with antenna and transmit-power models calibrated to public SpaceX filings. The results show that total capacity increases with beam count, but less than proportionally. With eight concurrent beams, BL-BnB improves mean per-beam capacity by 27.2% over nearest-satellite selection, primarily benefiting weaker links. BL-BnB achieves millisecond-scale runtimes in our evaluation, supporting the computational feasibility of optimal scheduling.

authors.name: Shizhen Jia, Hao Guo, Ruoyu Sun, Hans Geerdes, Mark Poletti, Songwei Dong, Lauryn Smith, Sundeep Rangan

papers.title: Improper Signaling for Clutter-Limited Angle Estimation in ISAC
papers.summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) transmit designs typically optimize the transmit covariance under proper signaling, leaving the potential sensing benefits of pseudo-covariance unexplored. This paper investigates the conditions under which transmit pseudo-covariance can influence the angle Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) of a deterministic target in the presence of clutter. For a prescribed transmit covariance and a single clutter patch, we establish that CRB sensitivity occurs if and only if the clutter is illuminated, exhibits nonzero non-circularity, and overlaps the angle-informative component of the target response. This characterization demonstrates that angular separation alone does not determine whether transmit impropriety can improve sensing performance. We derive a closed-form optimal incident-field pseudo-variance that minimizes the angle CRB over the set of feasible transmit pseudo-covariances. Under fully non-circular clutter scattering, the optimal design eliminates the clutter-induced CRB penalty. Numerical results for a 32-antenna ISAC system show CRB reductions of up to 99% relative to proper sensing under complete overlap and 30% under partial overlap, as well as up to approximately 7 dB lower clutter-induced CRB penalty across target-clutter separations. These findings identify transmit pseudo-covariance as a conditional sensing design resource whose effectiveness depends on clutter statistics and projected target-clutter geometry.

authors.name: Victor Augusto Del Monego, Poliana Basso, Murilo Capponi, Bruno S. Chang, Yahia Medjahdi, Giuseppe Thadeu Freitas de Abreu, Didier Le Ruyet

papers.title: Excitability of High-Frequency Positive Feedback
papers.summary: What is the threshold of an excitable system, i.e. the criterion that distinguishes rest from excitation? Previous research has shown that this question is far from trivial to answer. This paper studies the threshold of a simple excitable primitive in which excitability arises from the positive feedback interconnection of a first-order high-pass filter and a static, strictly monotone and strictly convex activation function. This threshold is a simple inequality on the difference between the instantaneous input and the motif's internal memory. While this result may help neuro-engineers characterize spiking in biological and artificial neurons, we argue that excitability is not always a desirable property, and that our threshold may also be relevant to safety considerations in fragile systems with rate-induced tipping points. We illustrate our framework with three examples: the FitzHugh-Nagumo model of neuronal dynamics, a model of stop-loss cascades in the stock market, and a social contagion model.

authors.name: Gustave Bainier, Arthur Fyon, Christian Fernandez Lorden, Alessio Franci

papers.title: Extremal-Phase-Guided Sequential Convex Optimization: Model Order Reduction
papers.summary: Fixed-order frequency-weighted H-infinity approximation is a nonconvex problem, and local optimization methods can be sensitive to initialization. We present extremal-phase-guided sequential convex optimization (EPGSCO) for stable fixed-order rational approximation. We introduce a novel phase-guidance technique motivated by the all-pass structure underlying optimal Hankel-norm approximation, with a phase template fitted to the error-magnitude derivative at dominant peaks. We integrate this guidance with dominant-peak selection, focused frequency grids, and adaptive pole-residue and polynomial-coefficient updates to address stagnation and improve approximation accuracy. CD-player examples and benchmarks with known optimal errors evaluate the algorithm against established methods. Comparisons with classical sequential convex optimization (SCO) under shared settings for the common components assess the combined contribution of phase guidance and adaptive frequency refinement. Results demonstrate improved accuracy in most of the tested cases and attainment of the known optimum from four tested initializations for a constructed order-42 benchmark, with additional computation in some cases.

authors.name: Mustafa O\u{g}uz Ye\u{g}in, Hitay \"Ozbay, Tom\'a\v{s} Vyhl\'idal

papers.title: Joint Association and Beamforming Design for Cooperative ISAC Systems
papers.summary: Cooperation among multiple base stations (BSs) improves both communication and sensing in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) networks. However, it requires deciding which BSs serve each communication user (CU) and each target, and how each BS beamforms. In this work, we consider joint BS-CU and BS-target association, and beamforming for a general cooperative ISAC system, overcoming prior simplifications such as single-user or target setups, fixed BS roles, coherent radar or separate waveforms. We maximize a joint communication rate and position Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB) based tradeoff utility while guaranteeing a minimum service per-CU using a data queue model. We develop a successive convex approximation (SCA)-based beamforming with closed-form updates. The discrete association problem is solved as an overarching layer using a low-complexity algorithm. Numerical results validate the effectiveness of the algorithm and unveil benefits of cooperative communication and sensing.

authors.name: Abhishek Rajasekaran, Mehdi Karbalayghareh, Xiaoyan Ma, David J. Love, Christopher G. Brinton

papers.title: Human Mobility Sensing Using Wall-Reflected Beamformed Millimeter-Wave Communication Signals
papers.summary: Existing millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication beam patterns spatially weight human-scattered signals and shape the received-power signatures induced by human motion. We exploit these beam-shaped signatures for device-free walkingpace and walk-direction classification using a wall-reflected 60.8-GHz link with closely spaced phased arrays and fixed communication beamforming vectors. Human movement alters the interference between wall-reflected and scattered signals, producing power oscillations surrounding a central blockage fade. A beam-dependent interference model provides a physical interpretation of these signatures. Using received-power statistics from a continuous-tone experiment, we extract fade duration for walking-pace classification and pre/post-fade asymmetries for walk-direction classification. Measurements comprise 144 crossings from three participants along perpendicular and diagonal trajectories. Under leave-one-participant-out validation, logistic regression achieves 86.1% binary and 79.2% three-class walking pace accuracy, and 77.1% travel-direction accuracy. The results demonstrate mobility sensing using fixed communication beams without channel estimation, Doppler processing, or dedicated radar hardware

authors.name: Tony DiMichele, Raees Matheen Mullah, Christian Lopez Garcia, Zahra Najafi, Mohammed E. Eltayeb

papers.title: Soft-Label Governance for Distributional Safety in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent AI systems exhibit emergent risks that no single agent produces in isolation. Existing safety frameworks rely on binary classifications of agent behavior, discarding the uncertainty inherent in proxy-based evaluation. We introduce SWARM (\textbf{S}ystem-\textbf{W}ide \textbf{A}ssessment of \textbf{R}isk in \textbf{M}ulti-agent systems), a simulation framework that replaces binary good/bad labels with \emph{soft probabilistic labels} $p = P(v{=}+1) \in [0,1]$, enabling continuous-valued payoff computation, toxicity measurement, and governance intervention. SWARM implements a modular governance engine with configurable levers (transaction taxes, circuit breakers, reputation decay, and random audits) and quantifies their effects through probabilistic metrics including expected toxicity $\mathbb{E}[1{-}p \mid \text{accepted}]$ and quality gap $\mathbb{E}[p \mid \text{accepted}] - \mathbb{E}[p \mid \text{rejected}]$. Across seven scenarios with five-seed replication, strict governance reduces welfare by over 40\% without improving safety. In parallel, aggressively internalizing system externalities collapses total welfare from a baseline of $+262$ down to $-67$, while toxicity remains invariant. Circuit breakers require careful calibration; overly restrictive thresholds severely diminish system value, whereas an optimal threshold balances moderate welfare with minimized toxicity. Companion experiments show soft metrics detect proxy gaming by self-optimizing agents passing conventional binary evaluations. This basic governance layer applies to live LLM-backed agents (Concordia entities, Claude, GPT-4o Mini) without modification. Results show distributional safety requires \emph{continuous} risk metrics and governance lever calibration involves quantifiable safety-welfare tradeoffs. Source code and project resources are publicly available at https://www.swarm-ai.org/.

authors.name: Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Raeli Savitt

papers.title: Algorithmic Authority and the Clinical Standard of Care
papers.summary: The integration of artificial intelligence into clinical medicine creates a fundamental tension between algorithmic probabilistic reasoning and the experiential intuition of expert physicians; applying Lawrence Lessig's \enquote{Code is Law} framework, I argue that the architecture of clinical AI systems already functions as de facto medical regulation, reshaping liability and the standard of care. Reframing AI \enquote{hallucination} as structurally analogous to well-documented human cognitive failures such as confirmation bias and premature diagnostic closure, I show that both failure modes demand a unified governance response. I therefore propose a dialectical standard of care that treats the integrated AI-physician dyad as the singular responsible diagnostic entity, mandating the synthesis of algorithmic precision with human interpretive authority within robust data governance and patient privacy frameworks.

authors.name: Aizierjiang Aiersilan

papers.title: The Confidence Score: a New Measure on Kernels
papers.summary: Across a wide range of applications, kernel measures are used to tune hyperparameters, select among candidate kernels, and assess the suitability of kernels for specific learning tasks. For classification, kernel measures are used to predict which kernels may produce accurate kernel classifiers. Many existing kernel measures, such as alignment to the ideal kernel, are designed to reward kernels which captures all samples from the same class as similar. While effective in many settings, this requirement is unnecessarily restrictive for classification, where classes may exhibit substantial internal structure. In this work, the "Confidence Score", a new kernel measure, is proposed. Unlike alignment-to-the-ideal kernel measures, the Confidence Score measures the alignment between an encoding of the ground truth and that ground truth projected by the kernel, allowing kernels that preserve intra-class structure to achieve high scores. Through experiments, it is demonstrated that the Confidence Score exhibits a higher correlation with classification accuracy across a variety of kernels on both real-world and synthetic datasets, compared to select other kernel measures.

authors.name: Elizabeth Hofer, Martin v. Mohrenschildt

papers.title: Exact signal recovery from generative priors with sigmoid output activation
papers.summary: We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[\delta, 1 - \delta]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/\delta)))$ measurements.

authors.name: Matthew S. Scott, Yaniv Plan, \"Ozg\"ur Y{\i}lmaz

papers.title: Translate, then decide: asymptotic optimality of latent-space control in bistable systems
papers.summary: This paper asks whether an optimal decision can be separated from the physical dynamics on which it acts. It studies this question through minimum-energy barrier crossing in scalar bistable systems. It characterizes the finite-horizon optimal feedback and shows that, as the horizon grows, it converges to a law that doubles and reverses the drift while it opposes crossing, and switches off once the barrier is passed. In physical coordinates, this law inherits the plant's nonlinearity, entangling decision and dynamics. We show that a plant-specific translation of state, input, and time maps every double well in the considered class to the same unit-rate linear world model, allowing a downstream decision stage to use a single plant-independent control primitive. This separation generally loses optimality at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve the physical control energy. Nevertheless, we prove that the excess physical energy of the layered controller vanishes as the horizon grows and that its limiting feedback reproduces the asymptotic optimum exactly. Thus, translation and optimization generally do not commute at a finite horizon, but commute in the asymptotic limit.

authors.name: Arthur Castello B. de Oliveira

papers.title: Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
papers.summary: Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.

authors.name: Andr\'e Tits, Pierre-Antoine Absil, No\'e Tits

papers.title: Hotplug Coded Caching: Embedding the YMA and Interference Elimination Schemes via Reed--Muller Codes
papers.summary: In the hotplug coded caching model, $K$ users fill their caches of size $M$ as a function of $N$ files, but only an unknown subset of $A<K$ users is active in the delivery phase. We recently showed that (i) under uncoded placement, offline users cause a strict load penalty at intermediate memory sizes, so that coded placement is needed; and (ii) for $AM\leq N$, every classical scheme with row-wise placement, including the scheme of Gomez-Vilardebo (GV), can be embedded in a Reed-Solomon code, which removes the penalty. In this note, we show that every point of the scheme of Yu, Maddah-Ali and Avestimehr (YMA) for a classical system with $A$ users is achievable in the hotplug model for every $K\geq A$. Each user is associated with a hyperplane and each file with a homogeneous polynomial; each user caches the restriction of the polynomial to its hyperplane, and the subfiles seen by the active users are the values of the polynomial at the points where their hyperplanes meet. This is a projective Reed-Muller code, which reduces to the Reed-Solomon code when each subfile is cached by one user. We then show, by an existence argument, that every classical scheme whose cache is a linear compression of the Maddah-Ali-Niesen cache and whose correctness holds for generic coefficients can also be embedded over a sufficiently large field; this includes the interference elimination (IE) schemes of Tian and Chen. These embeddings complement the Reed-Solomon one, which allows any row-wise placement and any delivery. Together with past work, our results show that every point attained by a GV, YMA or IE scheme ($N\leq A$ for IE), and every corner point of the linear tradeoff for $A=N=3$, is achievable in the hotplug model with a load that does not depend on $K$. Whether the optimal hotplug tradeoff depends only on $A$ remains open, but these results support a positive answer.

authors.name: Daniela Tuninetti

papers.title: ZipDrift: Generating Multimodal Short-Horizon MPC Costs with One-Step Drifting Models
papers.summary: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.

authors.name: Ke Zhang

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Sliding Mode Control for Robust Vision Stabilization under the Plant-Binding Condition
papers.summary: Boundary-layer Sliding Mode Control (SMC) has been applied to vision-based stabilization, but identifying its activation condition against simpler causal baselines (LPF, PID) has been elusive. The operational condition is plant binding: the disturbance velocity approaches or exceeds the actuator slew limit, so the bounded per-step actuation budget binds. We validate this in two independent vision domains: handheld translation stabilization (12 1080p clips; LPF, PID, SMC, L1) and angular re-framing against a virtual slew-rate-limited pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) plant. Outside binding, leave-one-out cross-validation makes SMC and LPF on translation statistically indistinguishable, and PID beats SMC on the angular 99th-percentile pointing offset by 5.85 degrees (95% CI clear of zero); inside binding -- reached only by sweeping the simulated slew limit, as both captured datasets land outside it -- the translation gap stays a tie and SMC beats PID on the angular worst case (Cohen's d up to +0.83). The PTZ plant's 100 degrees/s default sits on the cross-over, which explains a small-margin PID result previously reported in the angular setting. A complementary ablation shows raising the SMC reaching gain k costs mean tracking outside a narrow window.

authors.name: Sooyeun Yang, Jongseong Brad Choi, Seung Bok choi

papers.title: PRISM-AMC: Replay-Free Continual Learning for Automatic Modulation Classification
papers.summary: Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is a key component of cognitive wireless systems, enabling spectrum awareness and adaptive communication. Most deep learning approaches to AMC assume a fixed set of modulation classes and access to previously observed training data. In practice, modulation classes and channel conditions may evolve over time, while storage or data-retention constraints may preclude replay of raw baseband I/Q samples. We propose PRISM-AMC, a replay-free continual learning framework that mitigates catastrophic forgetting by preserving task-relevant subspaces of intermediate representations via gradient projection memory. We further analyze projected stochastic-gradient updates under an SNR-dependent gradient-noise model. PRISM-AMC is evaluated in both class-incremental and domain-incremental settings. Experiments on the MIGOU and DeepSig 2018.01A datasets show substantially reduced forgetting relative to sequential fine-tuning and elastic weight consolidation, while remaining competitive with or outperforming replay-based RSD-AMC in class-incremental settings, without storing raw I/Q samples.

authors.name: Usman Akram, Matthew Graham, Haris Vikalo

papers.title: A Layered View of LLM Support in Underwater Robotics
papers.summary: This extended abstract discusses a specific and, in our experience, practically relevant role for large language models (LLMs) in underwater robotics. Our main premise is that, in underwater fielding missions, the immediate difficulty is often not the synthesis of new low-level control laws, but the operation of complex robotic systems under limited communications, partial observability, and expensive field time. In particular, a significant fraction of the effort during sea trials is devoted to fault diagnosis, telemetry interpretation, mission adjustment, and coordination across heterogeneous assets and operators. We argue that LLMs may be useful at this higher operational level, especially when grounded in structured vehicle state, alarms, logs, mission context, and existing planning or validation tools. At the same time, current limitations in grounding, consistency, and causal reasoning make these systems lack the predictability required to guarantee direct control, especially in real-world critical applications, although we do not exclude a future evolution in this direction. This viewpoint suggests a layered architecture in which conventional autonomy remains responsible for control, perception, estimation, and validated mission execution, whereas LLM-based modules serve as an additional support layer for debugging, operator interaction, constrained replanning support, orchestration, and post-mission analysis.

authors.name: Federico Celi, Leonardo Zacchini, Gabriele Ferri

papers.title: SonoDyno: A Sonic Dynamometer for Engine Speed and Load Estimation from Audio
papers.summary: Controllable engine sound synthesis, Active Sound Design and engine order analysis all build on the relationship between the sound of an engine and its momentary operating state: its speed and its load. Recordings of engine sound are abundant in archives, sample packs and online video, yet they rarely carry time-aligned annotations of that state, which limits their applicability to controllable engine sound generation. We present SonoDyno, which estimates the engine speed, the cylinder count and an engine-normalized load intensity from a microphone signal alone, with no tachometer, no bus access and no prior knowledge of the engine configuration. A convolutional scorer of 124,302 parameters reads the harmonic order energy of each frame at three time-frequency resolutions to jointly score cylinder count and speed, and a decoder imposes the rotational dynamics of the engine on the speed trajectory. A second head estimates the load intensity, the position of the torque between the engine's drag floor at 0 and its full-load ceiling at 1, from the order levels at the decoded speed. On recordings of engines it has never heard, with microphone position, engine type and cylinder count unknown, SonoDyno places 93 to 97% of the frames within 2% of the true speed, identifies the cylinder count with 80% accuracy and confuses the octave on fewer than 2% of the frames. On an unseen engine of a known type, the load intensity has a mean absolute error of 0.12, and the sign of the torque, driving or braking, is right on 91% of the frames. General pitch trackers fall behind even when the harmonic order of each engine is supplied: on our validation recordings and at a tolerance of 5%, the best of them places 62% of the frames within the tolerance, against 96% for SonoDyno.

authors.name: Robin Doerfler, Beat Rossmy

papers.title: Consistency Learning and Distillation for One-Step MIMO-OFDM Channel Estimation
papers.summary: Iterative neural channel estimators can improve recovery under pilot contamination, but repeated network evaluations increase inference cost. This paper develops observation-anchored consistency and Consistency Mid-Training (CMT) estimators for one-step channel estimation in multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. Both estimators refine pilot-derived least-squares channel estimates in the delay-beam domain. Consistency learning couples endpoint predictions along noisy-to-clean paths. CMT then refines a compact consistency-trained student to predict a flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states. Across the evaluated SNR range, the compact CMT student reduces uncoded symbol error rate (SER) by 9.6-20.2% relative to the one-step flow-matching baseline (0.44-0.98 dB in logarithmic SER reduction), while using 74.5% fewer parameters and 73.0% fewer network multiply-accumulates.

authors.name: Fredrik Nguyen, Qiwen Wang

papers.title: Corridor-Based Monitoring and Emergency Braking Decision for Automated Vehicle Safety
papers.summary: This paper addresses emergency-braking decisions for a redundant safety channel in automated vehicles. The channel is responsible for identifying hazards from sensor data and determining whether braking is necessary, given the constrained computational resources of embedded hardware. We present an emergency-braking approach that uses a predicted motion corridor to filter \ac{lidar} measurements and then decide whether the ego vehicle must brake. \ac{pmcm} constructs a curvature-aware boundary from the planned path and vehicle geometry so that the monitored region contains the full swept body on both straight and curved paths. \ac{gdeta} then decides whether the ego vehicle must command an emergency brake for objects inside this boundary, scoring geometric occupancy and temporal urgency independently. Hard gates permit braking when either source is conclusive; soft-OR arbitration combines partial evidence when neither gate is active. Consecutive-scan confirmation reduces sensitivity to transient measurement noise. Corridor coverage is evaluated in controlled collision simulations and recorded campus driving. Braking decisions are evaluated in Monte Carlo simulations of lead-vehicle braking and transverse-crossing encounters.

authors.name: Junnan Pan, Vladislav Nenchev, Mohak Mansharamani, Prodromos Sotiriadis, Ferdinand Englberger

papers.title: Distributed Consensus, Optimization, and Learning under Communication Constraints
papers.summary: Many modern engineering applications require distributed problem-solving in which multiple nodes in a network cooperate to achieve a common optimization objective. Numerous distributed optimization and learning algorithms rely on consensus-based distributed coordination to ensure network-wide agreement via iterative local interactions. In these algorithms, the accuracy, frequency, and reliability of information exchange among network nodes directly influence system performance, including convergence behavior, training delay, and model accuracy. This tutorial article adopts a bottom-up approach to present the fundamentals of consensus averaging and distributed optimization methods, and highlights the impact of network connectivity, information flow, and communication uncertainty on network cooperation and optimization performance. Building on these theoretical insights, we discuss key design principles for communication-constrained distributed learning across diverse network topologies and review common approaches to communication-efficient learning, particularly in wireless networks. Despite substantial progress, further efforts are needed to bridge the gap between theory and practice and fully realize the potential of cooperative and networked intelligence.

authors.name: Zheng Chen, Nicol\`o Michelusi, Themistoklis Charalambous, Kaibin Huang

papers.title: To lift or not to lift: Operator inference for nonlinear PDEs with boundary control
papers.summary: Operator inference (OpInf) provides a nonintrusive framework for learning projection-based reduced-order models directly from data, but its standard formulations do not explicitly account for the fact that boundary actuation changes the admissible solution space of a PDE. This paper develops and evaluates a boundary-consistent, lifting-based OpInf formulation for nonlinear PDEs with time-varying inhomogeneous boundary conditions. The proposed approach decomposes the state into a known lifting component that satisfies the prescribed boundary conditions and a homogeneous component represented in a POD basis. Substituting this decomposition into the governing dynamics reveals a boundary-consistent reduced model structure in which the learned dynamics includes bilinear state-input and quadratic input-input interactions for quadratically nonlinear PDEs. The resulting operators are inferred from data, preserving the nonintrusive character of OpInf while guaranteeing boundary condition satisfaction by construction. Numerical experiments on boundary-actuated heat, Burgers, and lid-driven cavity problems show that the lifted formulation improves boundary compliance and can enhance prediction accuracy, solver stability, and computational efficiency, although these gains vary across problems and reduced model dimensions. Overall, this study establishes lifting as a principled extension of OpInf for boundary-actuated PDEs, clarifies when and how this formulation improves performance, and indicates that standard OpInf can remain an effective alternative in certain regimes.

authors.name: Zhuoyuan Wang, Yorie Nakahira, Wael H. Ali, Saviz Mowlavi

papers.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments
papers.summary: Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad. Results demonstrate that while encountering an unseen cross-current significantly increases an operator's physical and temporal demand, the introduction of haptic feedback mitigates these factors and improves self-assessed performance. Interestingly, the haptic condition also produced the highest levels of mental demand and operator frustration. Despite this increased mental workload, operators drove the ROV significantly faster when receiving haptic cues compared to the current-only condition, indicating a higher level of user confidence. Ultimately, these findings suggest that while haptic feedback may initially require more cognitive processing to interpret unseen hazards, it successfully enhances operator awareness and promotes more confident navigation in hazardous environments.

authors.name: Joshua Brown, Ildar Farkhatdinov, Michael Jenkin

papers.title: When to Ask for Help: Uncertainty-Triggered Aerial Refinement for Off-Road Navigation
papers.summary: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

authors.name: Pranay Samineni, Adam Thorpe, John Chubick, Anand Balakrishnan, Christian Ellis, Swarat Chaudhuri, Ufuk Topcu

papers.title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
papers.summary: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions require both semantic information reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy designs in SemCom mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source legitimacy. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation paradigm for integrated SemCom-identity protection to address active source impersonation and passive identity inference by treating each SemCom signal as an inherent carrier of both task-relevant semantic information and transmitter physical identity information. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for trustworthy decision making, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism under different operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic recovery quality is maintained to support anonymous sensing reports. The resulting outputs are jointly interpreted to support task decisions under mode-specific identity protection requirements. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.

authors.name: Yu Zhang, JingQi Liu, Shuangrui Zhao, Yuanyu Zhang, Yulong Shen, Xiaohong Jiang

papers.title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
papers.summary: Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation. Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference. Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed. Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

authors.name: Mohamed Azzam, Ziyang Xu, Quinlan Couch, Zoe Keese, Andrea Cadlo, Christine Sedze-DeWolf, Micaiah Uhrmacher, Madelyn Graff, Catherine Fox, Lauren Vatter, Paige Jeffryes, Jason Christensen, Neil Hamill, Shibiao Wan, Ling Li, Jieqiong Wang

papers.title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
papers.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $\epsilon$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $\epsilon\tau$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $\epsilon$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

authors.name: Kendra Givens, Taylor T. Johnson, Bryan C. Ward, Thomas Beckers

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Stochastic Optimal Control on Positive Cones
papers.summary: We consider stochastic optimal control problems in which the state is constrained to a proper cone. Specifically, we consider risk-neutral, risk-averse, and risk-seeking formulations within a single entropic-risk framework. We investigate classes of problems whose Bellman operator preserves affine functions and characterize their optimal value functions and feedback policies for both finite-horizon and time-average infinite-horizon problems. Additionally, we establish convergence and state-bound results under finite-step cost observability. Moreover, we demonstrate an exact connection between entropic-risk optimal control on proper cones and deterministic infsup control for systems whose dynamics and stage costs are affine in the disturbances. In addition, we provide examples of classes of systems for which explicit solutions can be obtained.

authors.name: Mohamad Al Ahdab, John-Josef Leth

papers.title: Landscape Analysis of Simultaneous Blind Deconvolution and Phase Retrieval via Structured Low-Rank Tensor Recovery
papers.summary: This paper studies the landscape of the simultaneous blind deconvolution and phase retrieval (BDPR) problem via a structured low-rank tensor recovery framework. Since the complicated sensing structure makes direct landscape analysis technically challenging, we introduce a tractable tensor sensing surrogate that preserves the essential low-rank structure. We first analyze its population risk, characterize the global landscape on the unit sphere, and establish local linear convergence of Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) under mild conditions. We then extend the analysis to tensor sensing under a tensor restricted isometry property (TRIP), establishing local geometric and RGD convergence guarantees, and quantify robustness to measurement noise. Our theoretical results are further supported by extensive numerical experiments. These findings offer insights into the optimization landscape of the surrogate tensor sensing problem, thereby providing guidance for studying and solving the original BDPR problem.

authors.name: Xiao Liang, Zhen Qin, Zhihui Zhu, Shuang Li

papers.title: Safety-Critical Control via Recurrent Tracking Functions
papers.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of synthesizing safety-critical controllers for high-order nonlinear systems, where constructing valid Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) remains computationally intractable. Leveraging layered control, we design CBFs in reduced-order models (RoMs) while regulating full-order models' (FoMs) dynamics at the same time. Traditional Lyapunov tracking functions are required to decrease monotonically, and systematic synthesis methods for such functions exist only for fully-actuated systems. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Recurrent Tracking Functions (RTFs), which replace the monotonic decay requirement with a weaker finite-time recurrence condition. This relaxation permits transient deviations of tracking errors while ensuring safety. By integrating CBFs for RoMs with RTFs, we construct recurrent CBFs (RCBFs) whose zero-superlevel set is control $\tau$-recurrent, and guarantee safety for all initial states in such a set when RTFs are satisfied. We establish theoretical safety guarantees and validate the approach through a proof-of-concept numerical experiment, demonstrating RTFs' effectiveness and the safety of FoMs.

authors.name: Jixian Liu, Enrique Mallada

papers.title: Game-theoretic Regulated Decentralized Coordination for Airspace Sector Overload Mitigation
papers.summary: Decentralized air traffic management systems offer a scalable alternative to centralized control, but often assume high levels of cooperation. In practice, such assumptions frequently break down since agents, each representing an airspace sector, may operate independently and prioritize local objectives. We address the problem of sector overload in decentralized air traffic management by proposing a regulated decentralized protocol that models self-interested behaviors based on best response dynamics. Each agent adjusts the departure times of its assigned flights to reduce its own congestion, without requiring centralized joint optimization. A tunable cooperativeness factor models the degree to which each agent accounts for overload in other sectors, while a minimal admissibility rule prevents local updates from creating new overloads. We show that this regulatory restriction is sufficient to guarantee finite-time convergence of best response dynamics to a pure Nash equilibrium under partial cooperation. In addition, we identify a sufficient condition under which an overload-free solution corresponds to a global minimizer of the potential function. Numerical experiments using one month of European flight data demonstrate that the proposed algorithm substantially reduces overload even with only minimal cooperation, achieving performance close to a centralized global mixed-integer optimizer and exceeding a centralized first-come-first-served baseline while requiring substantially less computation than centralized optimization. We further evaluate departure delay and fairness to quantify the operational cost of overload mitigation.

authors.name: Jaehan Im, Daniel Delahaye, David Fridovich-Keil, Ufuk Topcu

papers.title: Gap-Induced Sidelobes in Multiband Wi-Fi CSI and Their Impact on Multipath Delay Estimation
papers.summary: Leveraging channel state information from multiple Wi-Fi bands has the potential to improve delay resolution for ranging and sensing when wide contiguous spectrum is unavailable. However, non-contiguous spectrum access reshapes the spectral window, producing sidelobes and secondary peaks that can mask closely spaced multipath components. Prior work either designs the bands, which fixed Wi-Fi channelization does not allow, or addresses only the first multipath component. To characterize these secondary peaks, multipath delay estimation is studied in Wi-Fi-compliant multiband settings using channel state information. For a two-path model with unknown complex gains and delays, the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound for delay separation is derived and analyzed, confirming the benefit of larger frequency aperture at every separation considered, while revealing pronounced, separation-dependent oscillations driven by gap geometry and coupling of the two multipath components. Increasing aperture sharpens the mainlobe but also intensifies sidelobes and multipath interference, yielding competing peaks and a dominant peak shifted from the true delay. For the single-path matched filter, this shift is a deterministic offset governed by the slope of the autocorrelation function (ACF) of the allocation at the separation. A closed-form expression is derived for this offset, predicting it to within 21 ps for the analyzed channel combinations. Since the spectrum allocation enters both the bound and the offset, the impact of its gaps can be assessed for any legal aggregation before a measurement is taken.

authors.name: Ana Jekni\'c, Mihael Mohor\v{c}i\v{c}, Carolina Fortuna, Ale\v{s} \v{S}vigelj, Toma\v{z} Javornik, Andrej Hrovat

papers.title: Physical-Layer Anonymous Communication Design Under Symbol-Aware Identification and Transmitter-Dependent Noises
papers.summary: Physical-layer characteristics, such as channel state information (CSI) and transmitter noise induced by hardware impairments, are often uniquely associated with a transmitter. This paper investigates transmitter anonymity at the physical layer from a signal design perspective. We consider an anonymous communication problem where the receiver should reliably decode the signal from the transmitter but should not make use of the signal to infer the transmitter's identity. Transmitter anonymity is quantified using a Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD)-based metric, which enables the formulation of explicit anonymity constraints in the precoder design. We then develop a transceiver design that preserves reliable communication under spatial multiplexing while preventing transmitter identification. The proposed framework employs a partitioned equal-gain combining (P-EGC) scheme that leverages receiver diversity without requiring transmitter-specific CSI. Simulation results demonstrate anonymity-reliability tradeoffs across different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs), numbers of data streams, and alias selection methods. Moreover, the results reveal opposite trends of anonymity with respect to transmitter-dependent noise variations in the low-SNR and high-SNR regimes.

authors.name: Yu Li, Milad Tatar Mamaghani, Xiangyun Zhou, Nan Yang

papers.title: A Hetero-functional Graph State Estimator for Watershed Systems: Application to the Chesapeake Bay
papers.summary: Regional watersheds are systems of systems in which hydrology, land use, and governance interact. Nutrient models such as the Chesapeake Assessment Scenario Tool (CAST) route nutrients from land to the estuary through lumped delivery factors, so the river network that connects sources to the estuary is not represented explicitly. This paper develops a region-independent watershed reference architecture in Hetero-functional Graph Theory (HFGT) and adapts the Weighted Least Squares Error Hetero-functional Graph State Estimator to estimate nutrient flows in that network from uncertain data. The framework is applied to the Chesapeake Bay watershed. A mass-conserving network of land segments, outlet points, and river reaches is built from public geospatial data. CAST applied loads, land-segment edge-of-river loads, and river-to-bay delivery factors enter the estimator as measurements, each with its own error term. CAST-reported loads delivered to the Bay are withheld from estimation and used only to test the estimated delivery. The estimator reproduces the applied loads (R^2=1.00) and the land-segment edge-of-river loads (R^2=0.997) and under-predicts delivery to the Bay by 8.0% for nitrogen and 5.7% for phosphorus. The gap is traced to CAST delivery factors that imply in-river gains, which a mass-conserving network cannot represent, and to land segments whose edge-of-river loads exceed their applied loads. The framework provides a common systems representation for coupling watershed models with infrastructure, economic, and governance models.

authors.name: Megan S. Harris, John C. Little, Amro M. Farid

papers.title: A System-of-Systems Convergence Paradigm for Societal Challenges of the Anthropocene
papers.summary: Climate, water, food, energy and governance challenges are interdependent, yet the tools used to study and manage them remain divided by discipline and sector. Coupling sectoral models pair by pair cannot keep pace with the cross-sector and institutional interactions that drive global environmental change. In this Perspective we argue that convergence requires a shared system ontology that preserves meaning as knowledge moves from observation to computation and back to decision-making. Building on a meta-cognition map of scientific knowledge generation, we propose six design criteria for convergent system-of-systems approaches and assess four candidate methods against them, identifying model-based systems engineering paired with hetero-functional graph theory as a candidate "convergence spine". We illustrate the paradigm in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed, where a single ontology links nutrient-flow estimation, institutional analysis of restoration governance, team science and graduate education, and we distinguish what has been implemented from what remains future work. We close with implications for how global environmental change research is organized, funded and taught.

authors.name: Megan S. Harris, Mohammad Mahdi Naderi, Ehsanoddin Ghorbanichemazkati, Sina Jangjoo, Emily Lapan, Seyed Amirreza Hosseini, Fabian Schipfer, Stephen Craig, Enayat Moallemi, Inas Khayal, Laura M. Arpan, Tian Tang, John C. Little, Amro M. Farid

papers.title: Koopman Generator Decomposition for Port-Hamiltonian Systems
papers.summary: Port-Hamiltonian energy balance and Koopman approximation describe different aspects of nonlinear dynamics. This paper distinguishes exact observable identities, measure-dependent Galerkin projections, constrained surrogate identification, and certification of a controller on the nonlinear plant. Conservative weak skewness requires compatible measure and boundary conditions. Dissipative positivity belongs to the metric bracket; it does not generally make the projected first-order dissipative derivation positive. We give an explicit fixed-metric compatibility condition and a constant--Hamiltonian dictionary obstruction, and state the assumptions under which surrogate certificates imply plant bounds. A reproduced pendulum experiment illustrates the practical gap: its learned controller admits an exact shaped-energy certificate on the nonlinear plant, although its fitted quadratic storage is not a plant Lyapunov function and its archived residual-norm diagnostic is uninformative. These conclusions use the specified plant structure; they are not generic finite-data guarantees. The bracket, projection, and Lyapunov arguments are positioned relative to existing structured identification and residual-aware control methods.

authors.name: Victor M. Preciado

papers.title: Markov State-Space Modeling and Channel Characterization for DNA-Based Molecular Communication
papers.summary: DNA-based molecular communication with microarray-style reception under reversible hybridization is of interest for emerging DNA-enabled sensing and Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) systems. In such channels, the bound-state observation exhibits both inter-symbol interference (ISI) and colored counting noise. To capture these effects in a communication-oriented form, we develop a Markov state-space framework based on a voxelized reaction-diffusion model, in which a block-structured transition matrix describes molecular transport and binding/unbinding dynamics. For the microarray specialization, this representation yields the channel impulse response (CIR), the equilibrium gain, and a settling-time-based characterization of the effective channel memory. Building on the resulting symbol-rate observation model for on-off keying, we derive a grouped-binomial counting model and obtain a closed-form expression for the covariance of the counting noise. Based on these statistics, we further develop a differential-threshold detector and a finite-memory decision-feedback equalizer and benchmark them against a symbol-by-symbol maximum a posteriori detector with decision feedback (MAP-DF). Numerical results validate the theoretical correlation behavior and show that the relative performance of the proposed receivers depends strongly on the channel-memory regime.

authors.name: Ruifeng Zheng, Zhihan Xu, Veronika Volkova, Pengjie Zhou, Mart\'in Schottlender, Juan A. Cabrera, Frank H. P. Fitzek, Pit Hofmann

papers.title: On-Line Policy Iteration with Trajectory-Driven Policy Generation
papers.summary: We consider deterministic finite-horizon optimal control problems with a fixed initial state. We introduce an on-line policy iteration method, which, starting from a given policy, however obtained, generates a sequence of cost-improving policies and corresponding trajectories. Each policy produces a trajectory, which is used in turn to generate data for training the next policy. The method is motivated by problems that are repeatedly solved starting from the same initial state, including discrete optimization and path planning for repetitive tasks. For such problems, the method is fast enough to be used on-line. Under a natural consistency condition, we show that the sequence of costs of the generated policies is monotonically improving for the given initial state (but not necessarily for other states). We illustrate our results with computational studies from combinatorial optimization and 3-dimensional path planning for drones and a robot arm in the presence of obstacles. We also discuss briefly a stochastic counterpart of our algorithm. Our proposed framework combines elements of rollout and policy iteration with flexible trajectory-based policy representations, and applies to problems involving a single as well as multiple decision makers. It also provides a principled way to train neural network-based policies using trajectory data, while preserving monotonic cost improvement.

authors.name: Yuchao Li, Fei Chen, Yingke Li, Chuchu Fan, Dimitri Bertsekas

papers.title: Positivity of a Hadamard Product
papers.summary: A notable difference between the ordinary and Hadamard products is that the Hadamard product of two singular positive semidefinite matrices can be nonsingular. We present an eigenvalue lower bound for a Hadamard product that depends on a leading spectral projection of freely selected rank for one factor, and the smallest eigenvalues of certain principal submatrices of the other factor. Maximizing over the selected rank gives a stronger estimate; an effective-condition-number bound follows as a simpler consequence. We establish sharpness for prescribed ranks and effective condition numbers and examine limiting examples that delineate the bounds' usefulness.
